Decoupling Solving from Abstention: Single-Rollout Conformal Risk Control for Hard-Budget LLM Reasoning

Qianyi Chen    Bo Li ††thanks: Corresponding author: libo@sem.tsinghua.edu.cn. Affiliation: School of Economics and Management, Tsinghua University Affiliation:  GitHub     Hugging Face
Abstract

Reasoning with large language models (LLMs) relies on extended intermediate computation, so enforcing a hard token budget often exhausts the limit before an answer is produced. Forcing thinking to terminate recovers many correct solutions, yet it also exposes far more confident mistakes—turning budgeted reasoning into a coupled challenge of solving within the cap and deciding when to abstain. Existing approaches address these goals at high cost: supervised fine-tuning provides no deployment error bound, wrong-answer penalties in reinforcement learning (RL) can discourage weak solvers from attempting hard problems, and multi-sample conformal methods multiply inference compute. We introduce Tail-CRC, a single-rollout framework that decouples candidate generation from submission control. Tail-CRC first adapts a solver to a budget-forcing environment using pure binary correctness rewards, then freezes the solver and applies conformal risk control to the upper-tail token surprise of its answer span. A single trajectory supplies both the answer and its uncertainty score using only returned token log probabilities, yielding finite-sample control of expected wrong submissions under exchangeability while allowing risk targets or target domains to be recalibrated without retraining. Theoretically, we show how wrong-answer penalties introduce failure-only comparisons into group-relative RL, derive an exact exploration-starvation boundary in an attempt–solver learning model, and characterize length-induced ranking reversal and single-token spike sensitivity in answer scoring. Across Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3-8B on DAPO and out-of-domain Omni-MATH, 50 RL updates on 400 problems raise correct-submission rates by 15.0–29.6 and 4.3–12.8 percentage points over inference-only budget forcing while reducing generation cost by 3.5–12.6%. On 8B Omni-MATH, target-domain calibration lowers wrong submissions from 30.3% to 5.8% at a 4K budget and from 41.8% to 6.5% at 8K. Finally, 4K generation runs 2.05×\times faster for 4B and 2.23×\times faster for 8B than unforced 8K base decoding in local amortized batch time, demonstrating that decoupled solving and single-rollout calibration offer a practical path to reliable, efficient budgeted reasoning.

1 Introduction

Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning and adaptive test-time compute have substantially expanded what large language models (LLMs) can solve [34, 31], yet real deployments rarely offer an unbounded token budget. Under a hard output cap, a reasoning model must convert its intermediate derivation into a finished answer before tokens run out. This constraint turns inference into a three-way outcome: a correct submission, a wrong submission, or no submission at all. Standard accuracy treats the latter two identically, even though withholding an answer and exposing a confident mistake carry very different costs for downstream users. Reliable budgeted reasoning therefore requires solving two distinct problems: producing more correct answers within the cap, and deciding which completed answers are safe to submit.

Our evaluation of Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3-8B [27, 35] highlights how sharply these two goals collide. At a 4K token cap, uninterrupted Native decoding exhausts the budget without submitting an answer on 88.0–99.2% of problems across two mathematics benchmarks. Following s1’s budget-forcing strategy [25], injecting an end-of-thinking delimiter reserves tokens for answer synthesis and immediately recovers many solutions: on Qwen3-8B DAPO [36], correct submissions jump from 7.6% to 28.6%. At the same time, however, wrong submissions surge more than twentyfold, from 0.4% to 10.6% (Figure 1). Meeting the deadline does not eliminate failure; it shifts hidden truncations into visible errors.

Existing remedies struggle because they either leave deployment risk uncontrolled or pay a steep price in capability or compute. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can teach a model to reason from worked examples [25], but it leaves the deployment error rate uncontrolled. Incorporating wrong-answer penalties or abstention rewards into reinforcement learning (RL) couples caution directly into training [23]; under a hard cap, however, a weak solver can avoid penalties simply by exhausting the budget, starving itself of the very attempts needed to improve. Conformal methods can calibrate a rule for constructing candidate sets or aggregating reasoning paths [26, 12]. Each additional sample adds inference cost.

We instead decouple learning to solve from deciding when to abstain. We introduce Tail-CRC, a two-stage, single-rollout framework that keeps candidate generation and risk control separate. In the first stage, we train the solver inside the budget-forcing environment using RL with pure binary correctness rewards, encouraging it to finish as many correct solutions as possible within the cap. We then freeze the solver weights and apply conformal risk control (CRC) [3] to an uncertainty score computed from the upper tail of token surprises across the answer span. Because a single rollout supplies both the candidate answer and its score using only the token log probabilities routinely returned by hosted APIs, deployment requires no extra model calls and no auxiliary verifier. Under exchangeability, CRC guarantees finite-sample control of expected wrong submissions regardless of solver accuracy. Because calibration is decoupled from training, operators can change risk targets by adjusting the cutoff, or adapt to a new domain by recalibrating on a few hundred labeled target problems, without retraining the solver.

Figure 1 shows that Tail-CRC’s reliability gains do not come from trivially abstaining more. On DAPO at 4K, Tail-CRC actually submits more answers overall than both Budget forcing and Penalty RL (41.0% vs. 39.2% and 39.6% coverage), yet achieves higher correct submissions (33.9% vs. 28.6% and 29.4%) and lower wrong submissions (7.1% vs. 10.6% and 10.2%)—strictly dominating both baselines. On the harder out-of-domain Omni-MATH benchmark, Budget forcing and the unfiltered RL policies expose wrong answers on roughly one in five to nearly one in three problems (18.7–30.3%). There, Tail-CRC targets a 6.5% wrong-submission rate by withholding more predictions, cutting errors to 5.8% and more than doubling net score (R−WR-W) over Penalty RL (10.8% vs. 5.3%). When every penalty and explicit-abstention baseline is granted the same post-hoc tail-score calibration, Binary RL with Tail-CRC still achieves the highest net score across all twelve matched 4K comparisons (Section 5, Table 2).

Both halves of this design are grounded in concrete failure modes. On the training side, we show exactly how wrong-answer penalties activate failure-only group comparisons in group-relative RL, and derive a sharp exploration-starvation boundary in an attempt–solver model explaining how premature penalties can halt improvement. On the scoring side, relying only on final boxed-answer likelihood can miss uncertainty in the derivation and favor short wrong integers over longer correct symbolic expressions, while summing negative log likelihood (NLL) over the answer span introduces a length multiplier that can invert rankings altogether. Averaging the largest 10% of token surprises across the answer span removes this explicit length factor and limits the influence of any single lexical spike. As illustrated in Section 3.3 (Figure 3(b)), this allows Tail-CRC to preserve a correct radical answer rejected by Box NLL while filtering out a wrong integer that Box NLL confidently accepts.

The paper makes three contributions:

  • •

    A decoupled, single-rollout framework for hard-budget LLM reasoning. Tail-CRC separates binary-reward budget adaptation from answer-span CRC, providing finite-sample wrong-submission guarantees and retraining-free risk adaptation using one rollout’s returned token log probabilities.

  • •

    Theoretical mechanisms for training and single-rollout scoring. Exact group-advantage identities and an analytically solved attempt–solver flow explain penalty-induced exploration starvation, while score-anatomy results isolate length-induced ranking reversal and single-token spike sensitivity (complete proofs in Appendix A).

  • •

    Empirical gains in accuracy, controlled risk, and inference efficiency. Across Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3-8B, two domains, and 4K/8K budgets, 50 RL updates improve correct submissions by 15.0–29.6 and 4.3–12.8 percentage points over budget forcing while lowering generation cost by 3.5–12.6%; target calibration cuts 8B Omni-MATH errors from 30.3/41.8% to 5.8/6.5%, and local 4K generation runs 2.05×\times/2.23×\times faster than unforced 8K base decoding.

2 Problem Formulation

We study a reasoner that receives one problem, generates one trajectory within a hard token budget, and either submits its answer or withholds it. The objective is to retain as many correct submissions as possible at a chosen wrong-submission risk, with the generation cost of one rollout.

Budgeted generation.

Let xx be a problem, z⋆z^{\star} its reference answer, and πθ\pi_{\theta} an autoregressive model. A fixed stochastic decoder Kθ,B(⋅∣x)K_{\theta,B}(\cdot\mid x) generates trajectory yy under total token cap BB. Native decoding runs continuously; budget forcing reserves tokens for answer synthesis by inserting the end-of-thinking delimiter </think> if thinking exceeds its allocation. The answer span contains all sampled explanation and answer tokens after the first end-of-thinking delimiter and before end-of-sequence (EOS), whether thinking ended naturally or externally. Injected tokens and EOS are excluded from scoring. Exact 4K/8K allocations and early-ending rules are specified in Appendix B.

Outcomes and submission.

The observable indicator v⁡(x,y)v(x,y) records an EOS-terminated, extractable answer with consistent boxed contents. A valid candidate is right (Y=RY=R) or wrong (Y=WY=W) by mathematical equivalence; truncation, missing or conflicting answers, and explicit abstention give Y=UY=U. Labels require a reference answer during calibration and evaluation; validity and deployment selection do not. For a nonconformity score S⁡(x,y)S(x,y), larger means more uncertain, and invalid or empty spans receive S=+∞S=+\infty. We submit iff

gτ​(x,y)=𝕀⁡{v⁡(x,y)=1,S⁡(x,y)<τ}.g_{\tau}(x,y)=\mathbb{I}\{v(x,y)=1,\ S(x,y)<\tau\}. (1)

Define Rτ=P⁡(Y=R,gτ=1)R_{\tau}=P(Y=R,g_{\tau}=1), Wτ=P⁡(Y=W,gτ=1)W_{\tau}=P(Y=W,g_{\tau}=1), and Uτ=1−Rτ−WτU_{\tau}=1-R_{\tau}-W_{\tau}. Suppressing the cutoff subscript, coverage, net score, precision, and selective error are

C=R+W,Net=R−W,Prec=RR+W,rsel=WR+W.C=R+W,\qquad\mathrm{Net}=R-W,\qquad\mathrm{Prec}=\frac{R}{R+W},\qquad r_{\rm sel}=\frac{W}{R+W}. (2)

Marginal rates use all problem families; precision and selective error use submitted answers. Generation cost includes rejected trajectories. Rates are percentages; differences are percentage points (pp).

Calibration target.

The loss Lτ=𝕀⁡{Y=W,S<τ}L_{\tau}=\mathbb{I}\{Y=W,S<\tau\} records an exposed wrong answer. With the solver, decoder, validity rule, and score frozen independently of calibration, we select a cutoff from one rollout per labeled family so that

𝔼𝒟cal,test⁡[Lτ^]≤α.\E_{\mathcal{D}_{\rm cal},\,{\rm test}}[L_{\widehat{\tau}}]\leq\alpha. (3)

This expected marginal risk averages over calibration, a new test family, and stochastic generation; it differs from the error rate conditional on submission. Sections 3.1 and 3.4 give the construction and guarantee.

3 Tail-CRC: Method and Theory

3.1 Learning to solve before choosing when to submit

Tail-CRC first trains a solver to produce correct answers within the hard budget, then calibrates which candidates to submit. Separating these stages lets the submission rule adapt to a new risk target or population while keeping candidate generation fixed. Figure 2 summarizes the pipeline.

Binary RL uses terminal reward r0(Y)=𝕀{Y=R}r_{0}(Y)=\mathbb{I}\{Y=R\} in the same two-stage budget-forcing environment used at deployment. Dr. GRPO [22], a variant of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [30], centers each group of GG rollout rewards, Ag=rg−G−1​∑jrjA_{g}=r_{g}-G^{-1}\sum_{j}r_{j}, without standard-deviation normalization. Sampled thinking and answer tokens receive the terminal advantage with a fixed token denominator; deterministic prompt and injected delimiter tokens are masked. We freeze the final solver after training. The objective rewards a successful budgeted trajectory as a whole. Giving both sampled phases its terminal advantage allows training to improve the partial derivation and its final synthesis together. The learned solver thus supplies candidates before any deployment-specific choice about how many of their errors to expose.

A boxed answer can be a single confident token, whereas its preceding answer span exposes the transitions used to construct it. Let ℓt\ell_{t} be the negative log likelihood (NLL) of sampled answer token tt, after the first end-of-thinking delimiter and before EOS. Natural termination and budget forcing use the same span. Order the LL token surprises as ℓ(1)≥⋯≥ℓ(L)\ell_{(1)}\geq\cdots\geq\ell_{(L)}; Tail NLL is

S=1k​∑t=1kℓ(t),k=⌈0.1​L⌉.S=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{t=1}^{k}\ell_{(t)},\qquad k=\lceil 0.1L\rceil. (4)

The tail contains the largest surprises anywhere in the answer span. Invalid outputs and empty spans receive S=+∞S=+\infty. The API version uses token log probabilities from the generated trajectory; Tail entropy instead uses full-vocabulary entropy at the same prefixes (Appendix A.6.4).

With the solver, decoder, and score frozen, calibration generates and grades one trajectory per held-out family and applies standard CRC to choose a cutoff. Deployment generates one trajectory and submits it when it is valid and S<τ^S<\widehat{\tau}. References are needed for calibration; submission uses only the output and score. Changing the risk target changes the cutoff without retraining or extra generation.

3.2 Why binary rewards preserve learning opportunities

Under a hard cap, avoiding a wrong answer can mean exhausting the budget without submitting. To identify the training signal behind this behavior, consider Penalty RL rewards rλ​(R)=1r_{\lambda}(R)=1, rλ​(W)=−λr_{\lambda}(W)=-\lambda, and rλ​(U)=0r_{\lambda}(U)=0, for λ≥0\lambda\geq 0. Probabilities below refer to the actual stochastic rollout distribution.

Proposition 1 (Penalty signal and failure-only comparisons).

For G≥2G\geq 2 independent rollouts of a fixed prompt with probabilities (pR,pW,pU)(p_{R},p_{W},p_{U}), set γG=(G−1)/G\gamma_{G}=(G-1)/G. For outcomes of positive probability,

𝔼⁡[A1∣R]\displaystyle\E[A_{1}\mid R] =γG​(1−pR+λ​pW),\displaystyle=\gamma_{G}(1-p_{R}+\lambda p_{W}),
𝔼⁡[A1∣W]\displaystyle\E[A_{1}\mid W] =−γG​{λ⁡(1−pW)+pR},\displaystyle=-\gamma_{G}\{\lambda(1-p_{W})+p_{R}\},
𝔼⁡[A1∣U]\displaystyle\E[A_{1}\mid U] =γG​(λ​pW−pR).\displaystyle=\gamma_{G}(\lambda p_{W}-p_{R}). (5)

When pR+pW>0p_{R}+p_{W}>0, the last expression is positive exactly when pR/(pR+pW)<λ/(1+λ)p_{R}/(p_{R}+p_{W})<\lambda/(1+\lambda). For λ>0\lambda>0, a reward-varying group with no correct rollout has probability

(1−pR)G−pWG−pUG.(1-p_{R})^{G}-p_{W}^{G}-p_{U}^{G}. (6)

Every such group has zero advantages under binary reward. For any integrable per-rollout feature ψ\psi,

𝔼⁡[G−1​∑gAg​ψg]=γG​Cov⁡(rλ,ψ).\E\!\left[G^{-1}\sum_{g}A_{g}\psi_{g}\right]=\gamma_{G}\operatorname{Cov}(r_{\lambda},\psi). (7)

Proof. Appendix A.4 derives all three identities.

Non-submission has positive expected advantage below 50% submitted-answer precision for λ=1\lambda=1, or 20% for λ=0.25\lambda=0.25. Failure-only groups then favor UU over wrong attempts without containing a successful solution. Binary reward gives the whole group zero advantage. The comparison is prompt-specific: a difficult prompt can fall below the break-even precision even when the benchmark average is higher. A common non-submission reward 0≤ρ<10\leq\rho<1 is equivalent to effective penalty (λ+ρ)/(1−ρ)(\lambda+\rho)/(1-\rho) up to positive reward rescaling, which group centering retains (Corollary A.1).

An explanatory attempt–solver model connects this signal to learning opportunities. Let aa be attempt probability and qq success probability given an attempt, so (pR,pW,pU)=(a​q,a⁡(1−q),1−a)(p_{R},p_{W},p_{U})=(aq,a(1-q),1-a). The product Bernoulli mirror-gradient flow with relative solver learning rate κ>0\kappa>0 is

a˙=a⁡(1−a)​{(1+λ)​q−λ},q˙=κ⁡(1+λ)​a​q​(1−q).\dot{a}=a(1-a)\{(1+\lambda)q-\lambda\},\qquad\dot{q}=\kappa(1+\lambda)aq(1-q). (8)

Attempts decline below break-even precision while solver improvement slows with fewer attempts. For interior (a0,q0)(a_{0},q_{0}), λ>0\lambda>0, and q0<qc:=λ/(1+λ)q_{0}<q_{c}:=\lambda/(1+\lambda), starvation occurs exactly when

DBer(qc∥q0)≥−κlog(1−a0),D_{\rm Ber}(q_{c}\|q_{0})\geq-\kappa\log(1-a_{0}), (9)

where DBerD_{\rm Ber} is Bernoulli Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence. Then a→0a\to 0 and q→q∞≤qcq\to q_{\infty}\leq q_{c}, with finite total attempt and correct-rollout exposure; otherwise a,q→1a,q\to 1. Binary reward reaches (1,1)(1,1) from every interior initialization. Appendix A.4.4 proves the invariant and boundary cases for this specified flow.

Figure 3(a) shows the exact boundary at λ=1\lambda=1, κ=0.5\kappa=0.5: for q0=0.2q_{0}=0.2, recovery requires a0>0.36a_{0}>0.36. Starting at a0=0.25a_{0}=0.25 gives vanishing attempts and q∞≈0.309q_{\infty}\approx 0.309; starting at a0=0.50a_{0}=0.50 leads to recovery. The model explains how attempts can disappear before solver quality crosses break-even precision. The reward ablation tests the corresponding observable pattern: Penalty RL produces more truncation, fewer correct submissions, and longer rollouts (Table 2).

Equal rewards for explicit abstention and truncation express no preference between them: moving probability between these outcomes at fixed (pR,pW)(p_{R},p_{W}) leaves the objective unchanged. Rewarding explicit refusal alone would break that tie. Deployment selection is a separate choice: the optimal correctness threshold generally depends on both the target and population, even when posterior correctness is unchanged. Proposition A.1 in Appendix A.5 formalizes this dependence. Tail-CRC adjusts submission by recalibration; we compare training rewards after matched calibration.

3.3 Why score the upper tail of the answer span?

With the solver fixed, selection depends on score orderings. Box NLL omits the reasoning leading to an answer; Sum NLL incorporates that span but also its length; a maximum can be dominated by one unusual token. The following identities isolate these effects. For independent valid wrong and right draws, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) is AUC⁡(S)=P⁡(SW>SR)+12​P​(SW=SR)\operatorname{AUC}(S)=P(S_{W}>S_{R})+\tfrac{1}{2}P(S_{W}=S_{R}), with wrong answers as the positive class.

Proposition 2 (Length factor and ranking identity).

For a nonempty span, Ssum=L​ℓ¯S_{\rm sum}=L\bar{\ell}. With positive average surprises, define D=log⁡ℓ¯W−log⁡ℓ¯RD=\log\bar{\ell}_{W}-\log\bar{\ell}_{R}, Bℓ=log⁡LR−log⁡LWB_{\ell}=\log L_{R}-\log L_{W}, and ψ(u)=𝕀{u>0}+12𝕀{u=0}\psi(u)=\mathbb{I}\{u>0\}+\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{I}\{u=0\}.

AUC⁡(Ssum)=𝔼⁡ψ⁡(D−Bℓ),AUC⁡(ℓ¯)=𝔼⁡ψ⁡(D).\operatorname{AUC}(S_{\rm sum})=\E\psi(D-B_{\ell}),\qquad\operatorname{AUC}(\bar{\ell})=\E\psi(D). (10)

Proof. Appendix A.6.1 factors the pairwise comparison and gives a Gaussian surrogate for ranking reversal.

A correct symbolic derivation can have lower average surprise yet greater total surprise than a short wrong answer. Mean and tail averages remove the explicit length multiplier. Figure 3(b) illustrates a complementary problem with final-box scoring: it rejects a correct radical answer while accepting a confident wrong integer. Answer-span tail scoring reverses both decisions in these observed cases.

For Tk​(z)T_{k}(z), the average of the kk largest vector entries, the standard conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) representation [29] quantifies sensitivity to single tokens.

Proposition 3 (Tail aggregation and spike sensitivity).

For z∈ℝLz\in\mathbb{R}^{L} and k∈{1,…,L}k\in\{1,\ldots,L\},

Tk​(z)=minη⁡{η+1k​∑t=1L(zt−η)+}=max0≤wt≤1/k∑twt=1⁡w⊤​z.T_{k}(z)=\min_{\eta}\left\{\eta+\frac{1}{k}\sum_{t=1}^{L}(z_{t}-\eta)_{+}\right\}=\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}0\leq w_{t}\leq 1/k\\ \sum_{t}w_{t}=1\end{subarray}}w^{\top}z. (11)

This is empirical CVaR at tail mass k/Lk/L. A coordinate increase u≥0u\geq 0 changes TkT_{k} by at most u/ku/k.

Proof. Appendix A.6.2 proves the identities and bound, including ties, rounding, and replication effects.

The dual weights retain high-surprise transitions while capping each token’s influence at 1/k1/k; a maximum permits the full change uu. The mean weights every token equally; the tail concentrates on surprising transitions while averaging across them. These score properties hold regardless of autoregressive dependence. In the sparse-error explanatory model of Appendix A.6.3, tail averaging can improve separation by excluding background noise, whereas deterministic common background gives exact affine ranking equality with the mean. Small background variance relative to critical variance gives only a small standardized-separation gain, without establishing ranking equivalence. Empirically (Section 5), Tail NLL and Mean NLL perform comparably across our 36 model–domain–budget settings, splitting them 18–18, while both improve on Box NLL for 8B Binary RL on out-of-domain Omni-MATH.

3.4 Single-rollout finite-sample risk control

To calibrate submission, treat each problem family and its fixed-decoder output as one unit. Internal token dependence and variable trace length do not prevent exchangeability across families. Let nn be the calibration size, 0<α<10<\alpha<1 the marginal wrong-submission target, j=⌊(n+1)​α⌋j=\lfloor(n+1)\alpha\rfloor, and S(1)W≤⋯≤S(m)WS^{W}_{(1)}\leq\cdots\leq S^{W}_{(m)} the wrong calibration scores. The bounded-loss CRC rule [3] specializes to

τ^α={−∞,j=0,+∞,j≥1,m<j,S(j)W,j≥1,m≥j.\widehat{\tau}_{\alpha}=\begin{cases}-\infty,&j=0,\\ +\infty,&j\geq 1,\ m<j,\\ S^{W}_{(j)},&j\geq 1,\ m\geq j.\end{cases} (12)

Strict acceptance rejects cutoff ties. When j≥1j\geq 1, the rule allows at most j−1j-1 wrong calibration submissions, accounting for the finite-sample correction for the unseen family.

Theorem 1 (Single-rollout marginal risk control).

Let calibration and test families be exchangeable. Fix the solver, decoder, score, and verifier independently of these data. Applying the same stochastic kernel independently to each family preserves outcome–score exchangeability, and the cutoff (12) satisfies

𝔼𝒟cal,test⁡𝕀⁡{Ytest=W,Stest<τ^α}≤⌊(n+1)​α⌋n+1≤α.\E_{\mathcal{D}_{\rm cal},\,{\rm test}}\mathbb{I}\{Y_{\rm test}=W,\ S_{\rm test}<\widehat{\tau}_{\alpha}\}\leq\frac{\lfloor(n+1)\alpha\rfloor}{n+1}\leq\alpha. (13)

This holds at any solver accuracy, with one test trajectory.

Proof. Appendix A.1 proves decoder-preserved exchangeability and the rank bound, including ties.

The guarantee averages over calibration and test draws. Useful retention still depends on the solver supplying correct candidates and the score ranking them above wrong ones in confidence. For n=300n=300 and α=0.065\alpha=0.065, j=19j=19: at most 18 wrong calibration answers pass, and expected test risk is at most 19/301≈6.31%19/301\approx 6.31\%. A realized test-panel rate, or its confidence bound, can exceed the target. Choosing the largest admissible cutoff retains every lower-score candidate consistent with the corrected calibration count. Better discrimination therefore creates room for more correct submissions under the same risk rule. This separates two empirical questions: whether training increases the correct-candidate supply, and whether the score retains that supply when submission risk is controlled.

For source and target laws P,QP,Q with outcome–score marginals PZ,QZP_{Z},Q_{Z}, define FWP​(t)=P⁡(Y=W,S<t)F_{W}^{P}(t)=P(Y=W,S<t).

𝔼𝒟cal∼Pn⁡FWQ​(τ^α)≤α+supt{FWQ​(t)−FWP​(t)}≤α+TV⁡(PZ,QZ).\E_{\mathcal{D}_{\rm cal}\sim P^{n}}F_{W}^{Q}(\widehat{\tau}_{\alpha})\leq\alpha+\sup_{t}\{F_{W}^{Q}(t)-F_{W}^{P}(t)\}\leq\alpha+\operatorname{TV}(P_{Z},Q_{Z}). (14)

Proof. Appendix A.2 bounds the additional target wrong-answer mass below source cutoffs. Target-domain calibration restores the exchangeable setting without changing the solver. This motivates testing solver transfer and cutoff transfer separately: a model can retain its ability to solve target problems while the source cutoff admits too much of the target’s wrong-answer score distribution.

CRC controls marginal wrong submissions. Learn-then-Test (LTT) certifies error among submitted answers with high probability over calibration [2]. Even zero errors require 44 accepted examples for a 10% conditional-error target with ten fixed cutoffs and δ=0.1\delta=0.1. Appendix A.3 gives the test and Theorem A.1.

4 Experimental Setup

Models and controls.

We evaluate Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3-8B at total caps of 4K and 8K tokens [27, 35]. Binary RL uses 50 Dr. GRPO updates on 400 DAPO families: 16 prompts with eight rollouts each per update, or 6,400 trajectories per seed. Rank-32 LoRA [15] updates attention, MLP, and output projections. Training uses 4K external budget forcing, binary correctness reward, no KL penalty, and loss denominator 16×8×409616\times 8\times 4096; the final weights serve both caps. Controls are the pretrained model with Native decoding or Budget forcing, Answer-SFT, and Penalty RL (λ=1\lambda=1). Two ablations use Mild-Penalty RL (λ=0.25\lambda=0.25) or Explicit-Abstain RL, which adds an abstention instruction and action to the λ=1\lambda=1 reward. Binary RL has seeds 41 and 73; penalty arms use seed 41. All decoding uses temperature 1, top-p=0.95p=0.95, and top-k=20k=20. Tail-CRC filters Binary RL with calibrated Tail NLL.

Families and splits.

DAPO supplies 400 training, 200 development, 500 calibration, and 500 test families in disjoint panels [36]. Independent Omni-MATH confirmation uses 600 verifiable families absent from tracked prior panels, split into 300 calibration and 300 test families without answer-shape quotas [10]; test references include 37 bare integers and 263 other forms. To preserve blinding, all confirmation trajectories were generated before calibration labels were opened, and calibration cutoffs were locked before test labels were revealed. Native controls, additional penalty arms, white-box scoring, and DAPO Tail NLL analyses are supplementary studies on released panels; full protocols appear in Appendix B.

Estimation.

Binary RL averages its two frozen seeds within family, estimating single-seed deployment without answer aggregation. RR, WW, net score R−WR-W, and cost use all test families: 500 on DAPO and 300 on Omni; conditional error uses accepted submissions. Rates are percentages, absolute differences are percentage points (pp), and cost savings are relative to the stated comparator. AUROC uses valid right/wrong submissions with wrong answers positive; two-seed AUROC averages the seed-specific values. Pointwise 95% confidence intervals (CIs) use 20,000 paired family bootstrap resamples conditional on trained models and fitted thresholds; white-box AUROC uses up to 2,000 estimable resamples. Full estimation and calibration diagnostics appear in Appendices B and C.

5 Results

5.1 Q1: Does budget adaptation improve solving?

Binary RL increases correct submissions over Budget forcing in all eight settings, by 15.0–29.6 pp for 4B and 4.3–12.8 pp for 8B, with positive paired lower bounds throughout (Figure 1, Table 1). Budget forcing itself recovers completed answers but also exposes errors: across the four 8B domain/cap settings, it produces 6.3–26.5 times as many wrong submissions as Native. Binary RL’s API generation cost per family falls by 3.5–12.6% against the same-budget comparator. At 4K, its correct-submission gains over Answer-SFT are 12.30/8.33 pp on DAPO/Omni for 4B and 5.80/7.33 pp for 8B. The independent Omni-MATH confirmation validates both these solving gains and the score ranking analyzed next.

Training-time penalties trade away correct answers without directly setting deployment risk. On 8B DAPO 4K, Penalty RL lowers WW from Binary RL’s 18.9% to 10.2%, but also lowers RR from 41.4% to 29.4%. Truncation rises from 36.1% to 58.2%, and sampled output length from 3,423 to 3,628 tokens per family. This pattern is consistent with the incentive isolated in Proposition 1. Explicit-Abstain RL uses its added action on 0.6%/1.0% of DAPO families at 4K/8K, versus 10.0%/14.3% on Omni. Of its 43 Omni 8K abstentions, Penalty RL had answered 11 correctly; among its remaining submissions, 50.5% are wrong. The added action therefore trades away some correct answers while leaving substantial accepted error.

Giving every competitor the same calibration procedure preserves the main ordering. At 4K, Tail-CRC has higher net-score point estimates than all three separately calibrated penalty baselines in all twelve comparisons: two domains, three arms, and targets α=0.065/0.10\alpha=0.065/0.10. Against Penalty RL, the gains at these two targets are 7.20/9.00 pp on DAPO and 2.50/0.33 pp on Omni. Against Explicit-Abstain RL and Mild-Penalty RL, the four DAPO gains are 5.00–9.40 pp, all with positive paired lower bounds; the four Omni gains are 2.50–4.33 pp, with intervals crossing zero. Section 7 discusses the 8K Omni boundary.

Complementing these operating points, Binary RL’s observed selection frontier dominates seven of eight raw ablation points (Figure 4). Solving and adjustable selection are useful separate controls; a fixed reward penalty does not replace either.

5.2 Q2: Which single-rollout score supports selection?

In an earlier preregistered DAPO study using Box NLL, the 8B model missed its joint risk-and-gain gates (Appendix B.5), motivating our shift to answer-span tail scoring. Box NLL loses information when correctness depends on a long or symbolic answer. The observed cases in Figure 3(b) illustrate this mismatch; the independent Omni test quantifies it. For 8B Binary RL, Tail NLL versus Box NLL AUROCs are 0.756 versus 0.628 at 4K and 0.724 versus 0.622 at 8K. The paired improvements are 0.128 (95% CI [0.043,0.216][0.043,0.216]) and 0.102 ([0.025,0.180][0.025,0.180]). Under source-calibrated cuts at α=0.065\alpha=0.065, accepted correct answers whose references are not written as a single integer increase from 42 to 90 at 4K and 44 to 94 at 8K, across 526 seed–family records (263 families, two seeds).

Sum NLL has a separate length problem: its AUROC is 0.111 for the 4B Budget forcing baseline on DAPO 4K and 0.289 for Answer-SFT. Proposition 2 isolates this multiplicative length confounding. Across 36 model–domain–budget cells (nine model arms ×\times two domains ×\times two caps; Table 7), Tail NLL and Mean NLL have AUROC ranges 0.630–0.862 and 0.626–0.854, respectively. Tail NLL wins 18 cells and loses 18, so the two normalized scores perform comparably across these settings. Tail NLL’s demonstrated strength is correcting the Box NLL and Sum NLL failures (Figure 5).

What white-box access adds.

Full-vocabulary access provides an optional score upgrade. Replaying 28,800 trajectories and 15,461,536 valid answer tokens finds seven significant Tail entropy gains: six 8B DAPO cells and one 4B DAPO cell. The other intervals cross zero, including all 18 Omni cells. At 8B DAPO 8K, replacing Tail NLL with Tail entropy at α=0.065\alpha=0.065 raises Binary RL’s RR from 39.1% to 43.7%, changes WW from 5.9% to 6.2%, and raises net score from 33.2% to 37.5%.

Writing ptp_{t} for the model’s next-token distribution at step tt and YtY_{t} for the sampled token, sampled surprise decomposes as −log⁡pt​(Yt)=H⁡(pt)+bt+ξt-\log p_{t}(Y_{t})=H(p_{t})+b_{t}+\xi_{t}, where H⁡(pt)H(p_{t}) is full-vocabulary Shannon entropy, btb_{t} is predictable drift from the truncated decoder, and ξt\xi_{t} is conditionally centered sampling noise. Under raw-model sampling, the conditional variance of ξt\xi_{t} is varentropy. Tail selection can retain extreme drift or noise as well as entropy, so tokenwise centering does not equate the tail scores. Appendices A.6.4 and A.6.5 give the decomposition and its pathwise bound.

5.3 Q3: How do calibration and cost affect deployment?

Target calibration substantially reduces exposed errors. On 8B Omni, Tail-CRC at α=0.065\alpha=0.065 lowers WW from 30.33% to 5.83% at 4K and from 41.83% to 6.50% at 8K, while net score rises from −1.00%-1.00\% to 10.83% and from −3.00%-3.00\% to 11.50%. Source-calibrated cuts transfer less effectively: they accept every valid 4B Binary RL Omni output, giving W=9.83%W=9.83\% at 4K and 12.83% at 8K. Under transferred source cuts on 8B Omni, Tail NLL improves net score over Box NLL at 8K (+5.17 pp, 95% CI [0.33,10.17][0.33,10.17]), but its 4K interval crosses zero (+3.50 pp, [−1.00,8.33][-1.00,8.33]; Appendix B.5).

Among 36 target-calibrated settings (nine individual models, two caps, targets α=0.065/0.10\alpha=0.065/0.10), 28 realized test wrong-submission rates meet target. Across 2,000 finite-pool splits at 8B 4K and α=0.065\alpha=0.065, mean WW is 6.41% on DAPO and 6.31% on Omni (Figure 6). Conditional certification needs enough accurate accepted answers: Tail NLL issues 49/72 certificates in the retrospective DAPO analysis, while Tail NLL and Mean NLL each issue 3/72 on independently registered Omni grids, all at a 30% conditional-error target. Appendix C gives full counts and calibration-size sensitivity.

The cost trade-off depends on model size. Against Native 8K of the same size, 4K Tail-CRC raises 4B net score by 36.30 pp ([31.70,40.80][31.70,40.80]) on DAPO and 5.83 pp ([2.33,9.50][2.33,9.50]) on Omni, while API cost falls 47.4%/45.1%. The 8B cost savings are 43.0%/44.3%, but net-score differences are −7.80-7.80 pp ([−11.80,−3.80][-11.80,-3.80]) and −1.83-1.83 pp ([−5.83,2.17][-5.83,2.17]), respectively.

The models differ in how often they finish within 8K: 4B Native 8K still truncates 92.6% of DAPO and 91.0% of Omni trajectories, giving budget adaptation room to improve both net score and cost. In contrast, 8B Native 8K already solves 35.4% of DAPO problems with 97.8% submission precision; 4K Tail-CRC exchanges some net score for 2.23×\times faster generation and 43.0% lower API cost.

On vLLM [19], 4K Binary RL is 2.05×\times faster (4B) and 2.23×\times faster (8B) than Native 8K; 8B Binary RL at 8K uses 12.56% less generation time than Native 8K (Table 3). Comparing an already computed score with its threshold takes about 26 ns per family.

With Tail entropy at α=0.065\alpha=0.065, 8B Binary RL on DAPO 8K achieves R/W/Net=43.7/6.2/37.5%R/W/\mathrm{Net}=43.7/6.2/37.5\%, versus 35.4/0.8/34.6%35.4/0.8/34.6\% for Native 8K. The post hoc paired differences are Δ​R=+8.3\Delta R=+8.3 pp ([4.6,12.0][4.6,12.0]), Δ​W=+5.4\Delta W=+5.4 pp ([3.8,7.0][3.8,7.0]), and Δ​Net=+2.9\Delta\mathrm{Net}=+2.9 pp ([−1.3,7.0][-1.3,7.0]), all with 95% CIs. It submits more correct answers and more errors; the net-score interval crosses zero. Note that the 12.56% generation-time reduction above excludes the offline pass required to extract full-vocabulary entropy.

6 Related Work

Reasoning under a compute budget.

CoT prompting and self-consistency use intermediate computation and multiple reasoning paths [34, 33]; test-time scaling studies how to allocate that computation [31]. STaR trains on self-generated rationales that yield correct answers [37]. Rationale distillation uses teacher-generated explanations as supervision [14], and RL can build reasoning behavior directly [7]. For explicit budgets, s1 introduces inference-time forcing, L1 trains for chosen lengths, and ThinkPrune trains under a token limit [25, 1, 13]. Tail-CRC couples budget adaptation to a separate decision about which completed answers a deployment should expose.

Learning abstention.

The reject option and selective classification formalize prediction with withholding [6, 11]. Refusal-Aware Instruction Tuning (R-Tuning) teaches uncertainty responses [38]; reinforced hesitation distinguishes correct, incorrect, and abstaining outputs through rewards [23]. Our analysis isolates how these rewards interact with hard-budget non-submission under GRPO and Dr. GRPO [30, 22, 39]. Matched calibration tests which training objective supplies better answers at the same risk target.

Conformal control of generated outputs.

Conformal prediction calibrates set coverage [32, 20]; risk-controlling prediction sets and CRC extend calibration to loss targets [4, 3], while LTT tests candidate policies for risk certification [2]. Table 4 compares the decisions these methods calibrate.

Language-generation methods control candidate-set success, retained claims, or an answer aggregated from several paths. Tail-CRC controls the wrong-submission event from a single budget-adapted trajectory, using its answer-span token probabilities.

Uncertainty from one response or several.

Confidence can come from answer probabilities, self-evaluation, or verbal uncertainty [16, 17, 21, 28]. Semantic entropy compares meaning across sampled answers [8]; Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf) filters parallel reasoning traces by token confidence [9]. Our single-rollout comparison separates representation and length effects from the choice of token aggregation. CVaR supplies a precise tail-score interpretation [29]; the entropy extension relates sampled surprise to decoder drift and token varentropy [18].

7 Discussion and Limitations

Three deployment controls.

Training supplies correct candidates, scoring separates them from errors, and calibration sets the marginal wrong-submission target. Binary RL with Tail-CRC is useful under tight budgets and API log-probability access. Tail entropy improves the demonstrated 8B DAPO operating point when full-vocabulary access is available. With costly errors and an 8K budget, conservative Native decoding remains competitive. The deployment choice therefore depends jointly on RR, WW, and cost.

The precision boundary.

Calibration cannot create correct answers or recover separation absent from the score. On 8B Omni at α=0.065\alpha=0.065, Tail-CRC’s 4K net-score gains over identically calibrated Budget forcing and Answer-SFT are 0.17 and 0.50 pp; at 8K it retains 4.0 pp fewer correct answers than calibrated Penalty RL ([−7.67,−0.33][-7.67,-0.33] pp). Better raw solving does not guarantee the best small accepted subset. Likewise, the sparse-signal model provides a conditional explanation for tail scoring, and the evaluated 10% fraction is not universally optimal. The 18–18 Tail/Mean NLL split leaves both normalized scores viable. Similarly, white-box score gains do not identify decoder drift or varentropy as their cause, and zero-crossing intervals do not establish score equivalence.

Experimental scope.

The study covers two Qwen model generations and two verifiable mathematics domains. Binary RL has two training seeds; penalty arms have one, and Explicit-Abstain RL changes instruction and parser together. Equal zero rewards for refusal and truncation leave their relative value unspecified; rewarding prompt refusal would be a different intervention. The solved dynamics isolate a mechanism rather than identify the actual AdamW trajectory. A longer-budget Native-GRPO training control remains untested. Small exploratory training and two-draw studies are confined to Appendix D.

Calibration and systems scope.

Guarantees require the stated calibration/deployment relationship and correct labels. Three hundred reference-keyed calibration examples cost an estimated $0.73 for 8B or $1.31 for 4B at single-seed 4K generation rates; trustworthy labels in open-ended domains may be harder to obtain. Public-benchmark pretraining exposure is unknown, and supplementary released-panel analyses are not independent confirmations. At a matched 4K cap, extra prefill can make budget forcing slightly more expensive than Native; rejection refunds no generated tokens. Full-vocabulary extraction remains untimed, and open-engine reconstruction does not establish identical generation distributions. Future work can improve solvers, trajectory ranking, and calibration under shift.

Appendix A Complete proofs and theoretical extensions

The first three sections establish finite-sample guarantees. The next sections prove the reward and score results and their explanatory models. Counterexamples clarify the assumptions behind each conclusion.

A.1 Proof of Theorem 1

Step 1: preserve exchangeability through the decoder.

Let FiF_{i} be the complete problem family and K(⋅∣Fi)K(\cdot\mid F_{i}) the fixed kernel for trajectory generation, budget forcing, score extraction, and outcome grading. The distribution of ((,,,,,))i=1n+1((F_{i},Y_{i},S_{i}))_{i=1}^{n+1} integrates the product ∏iK⁡(d​yi,d​si∣Fi)\prod_{i}K(dy_{i},ds_{i}\mid F_{i}) against the exchangeable law of (Fi)i=1n+1(F_{i})_{i=1}^{n+1}. Permuting all indices leaves both factors unchanged. Therefore the augmented observations are exchangeable. Token dependence, stochastic decoding, and deterministic external delimiters are internal to KK; they do not change this argument. Independent random seeds across families implement the product-kernel assumption; pairing seeds across comparison arms preserves each arm’s argument.

Step 2: reduce calibration to a rank rule.

Write N=n+1N=n+1 and define Zi=SiZ_{i}=S_{i} when Yi=WY_{i}=W, and Zi=+∞Z_{i}=+\infty otherwise. For j=⌊N​α⌋≥1j=\lfloor N\alpha\rfloor\geq 1, the threshold from nn calibration observations is their jjth ordered ZZ value: when fewer than jj wrong scores are finite, it is +∞+\infty. Since α<1\alpha<1, j≤nj\leq n. For each i≤Ni\leq N, let Z(j)−iZ_{(j)}^{-i} be the jjth order statistic after omitting ii, and set

Ei=𝟏​{Yi=W,Zi<Z(j)−i}.E_{i}=\mathbf{1}\{Y_{i}=W,\ Z_{i}<Z_{(j)}^{-i}\}.

For any deterministic collection of NN observations,

∑i=1NEi≤j.\sum_{i=1}^{N}E_{i}\leq j. (A.1)

To see this with ties, group finite wrong scores by value. A score in a group whose cumulative count is rr is strictly below the jjth leave-one-out value only if r≤jr\leq j: the other r−1r-1 observations at or below that value would otherwise already fill the first jj ranks. Thus only entire groups contained within the first jj ranks can count. If there are at most jj finite wrong scores, all of them can count and their number is still at most jj. Infinite scores never satisfy a strict comparison with an infinite threshold.

Step 3: average over the test position.

Exchangeability gives 𝔼​EN=N−1​𝔼​∑iEi\mathbb{E}E_{N}=N^{-1}\mathbb{E}\sum_{i}E_{i}. Equation (A.1) yields 𝔼​EN≤j/N≤α\mathbb{E}E_{N}\leq j/N\leq\alpha. When j=0j=0, the declared reject-all rule has risk zero. This proves every case in (12). If all wrong scores are finite and almost surely distinct, and MWM_{W} is the number of wrong outputs among all NN observations, the proof additionally gives the exact identity

𝔼​EN=𝔼⁡[min⁡{j,MW}]N.\mathbb{E}E_{N}=\frac{\mathbb{E}[\min\{j,M_{W}\}]}{N}.

Consequently the rule can accept every valid answer when wrong outputs are already rare; reaching the risk target is not required for validity.

Step 4: relation to the corrected empirical risk.

For j≥1j\geq 1, the inequality 1+∑i𝟏​{Yi=W,Si<τ}≤N​α1+\sum_{i}\mathbf{1}\{Y_{i}=W,S_{i}<\tau\}\leq N\alpha is equivalent to allowing at most j−1j-1 calibration wrong submissions. The largest admissible threshold is the jjth wrong score, unless fewer than jj such scores exist, in which case all finite valid scores can pass. With strict acceptance, 𝟏{S<τ}\mathbf{1}\{S<\tau\} is left-continuous in τ\tau, and a tied threshold rejects the entire tie group. The rank proof above avoids any continuity assumption. ∎

A.2 Risk under shift, repeated test items, and seed averaging

For any fixed threshold tt, FWQ​(t)≤FWP​(t)+dWF_{W}^{Q}(t)\leq F_{W}^{P}(t)+d_{W} where dW=supt(FWQ​(t)−FWP​(t))d_{W}=\sup_{t}(F_{W}^{Q}(t)-F_{W}^{P}(t)). Taking the expectation over a source calibration set and using Theorem 1 proves the first inequality in (14); the second follows because each event {Y=W,S<t}\{Y=W,S<t\} is measurable and bounded by total variation. When both domains use the same decoder and verifier kernel, the data-processing inequality further bounds induced total variation by that between the complete problem-family distributions. The bound is an expectation over calibration sets; it does not assert FWP​(τ^)≤αF_{W}^{P}(\widehat{\tau})\leq\alpha for every realized calibration split.

If calibration and the mm future test families are jointly exchangeable, linearity gives 𝔼⁡[m−1​∑i=1mLi​(τ^)]≤α\mathbb{E}[m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{m}L_{i}(\widehat{\tau})]\leq\alpha. Under i.i.d. test draws, conditionally on calibration this test average has mean FWP​(τ^)F_{W}^{P}(\widehat{\tau}) and variance FWP​(τ^)​(1−FWP​(τ^))/mF_{W}^{P}(\widehat{\tau})(1-F_{W}^{P}(\widehat{\tau}))/m. The conditional mean itself varies with calibration. This is why an empirical test rate or its one-sided confidence limit can exceed α\alpha without contradicting the expected-risk statement.

If two frozen training seeds are calibrated separately and one is selected uniformly for deployment, the deployed risk is the average of their risks. Linearity preserves the same expected-risk bound. Reporting this average within each family estimates the randomized single-seed deployment policy; it is not a two-rollout voting procedure, and the seeds do not double the independent family count.

A.3 Conditional selective-error certificate and proof

Fix a solver, decoder, verifier, score, and calibration-independent grid Λ\Lambda of MM cutoffs, a selective-error target αsel∈(0,1)\alpha_{\rm sel}\in(0,1), and error probability δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1). For nn calibration families, define

Nτ=∑i=1n𝕀{Si<τ},Wτ=∑i=1n𝕀{Yi=W,Si<τ}.N_{\tau}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{I}\{S_{i}<\tau\},\qquad W_{\tau}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{I}\{Y_{i}=W,S_{i}<\tau\}.

The one-sided exact binomial test is

pτ=Pr{Bin(Nτ,αsel)≤Wτ},pτ=1if Nτ=0.p_{\tau}=\Pr\{\operatorname{Bin}(N_{\tau},\alpha_{\rm sel})\leq W_{\tau}\},\qquad p_{\tau}=1\ \text{if }N_{\tau}=0. (A.2)
Theorem A.1 (Fixed-grid selective-error certificate).

Let calibration families and an independent test family be independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.). Apply the same frozen decoding kernel independently to each family, with the score and grid fixed independently of these data. Select the largest τ∈Λ\tau\in\Lambda satisfying pτ≤δ/Mp_{\tau}\leq\delta/M, or issue no certificate. With probability at least 1−δ1-\delta over calibration, every issued cutoff has P⁡(Ytest=W∣Stest<τ^,𝒟cal)≤αselP(Y_{\rm test}=W\mid S_{\rm test}<\widehat{\tau},\mathcal{D}_{\rm cal})\leq\alpha_{\rm sel}.

Proof. The conditional binomial argument and simultaneous testing steps follow.

Step 1: condition on the accepted sample size.

For a fixed calibration-independent threshold τ\tau, set Ai=𝟏{Si<τ}A_{i}=\mathbf{1}\{S_{i}<\tau\} and Bi=𝟏​{Yi=W,Si<τ}B_{i}=\mathbf{1}\{Y_{i}=W,S_{i}<\tau\}. Under i.i.d. families the pairs (Ai,Bi)(A_{i},B_{i}) are i.i.d. If cτ=P⁡(Ai=1)>0c_{\tau}=P(A_{i}=1)>0, then conditioning on the set of accepted indices makes their wrong indicators independent Bernoulli variables with common parameter rτ=P⁡(Bi=1∣Ai=1)r_{\tau}=P(B_{i}=1\mid A_{i}=1). Hence

Wτ|Nτ=k∼Bin⁡(k,rτ).W_{\tau}\mid N_{\tau}=k\sim\operatorname{Bin}(k,r_{\tau}).

If cτ=0c_{\tau}=0, Nτ=0N_{\tau}=0 almost surely and the threshold cannot be certified.

Step 2: verify each p-value.

Let Fk,aF_{k,a} be the binomial CDF with parameters (k,a)(k,a). For rτ≥a=αselr_{\tau}\geq a=\alpha_{\rm sel} and u∈[0,1]u\in[0,1], the event Fk,a​(Wτ)≤uF_{k,a}(W_{\tau})\leq u is a lower-tail event Wτ≤bW_{\tau}\leq b for some integer bb, or is empty. By binomial stochastic ordering, a larger parameter has no larger lower-tail probability:

Prτ​{Fk,a​(Wτ)≤u∣Nτ=k}≤Fk,a​(b)≤u.P_{r_{\tau}}\{F_{k,a}(W_{\tau})\leq u\mid N_{\tau}=k\}\leq F_{k,a}(b)\leq u.

The k=0k=0 convention pτ=1p_{\tau}=1 is valid as well. Averaging over NτN_{\tau} proves super-uniformity under every bad threshold with rτ>αselr_{\tau}>\alpha_{\rm sel}.

Step 3: control every selected threshold.

Let Λbad={τ∈Λ:rτ>αsel}\Lambda_{\rm bad}=\{\tau\in\Lambda:r_{\tau}>\alpha_{\rm sel}\}. A union bound yields

P⁡{∃τ∈Λbad:pτ≤δ/M}≤|Λbad|​δ/M≤δ.P\{\exists\tau\in\Lambda_{\rm bad}:p_{\tau}\leq\delta/M\}\leq|\Lambda_{\rm bad}|\delta/M\leq\delta.

Outside this event, all passing thresholds have conditional error at most αsel\alpha_{\rm sel}, so selecting the largest one is valid. No monotonicity of rτr_{\tau} is needed. If none passes, no conditional-risk certificate is issued. The independent future family’s risk conditional on calibration and the selected threshold is rτ^r_{\widehat{\tau}}. ∎

Accepted-volume requirement.

At Wτ=0W_{\tau}=0, the p-value is (1−αsel)Nτ(1-\alpha_{\rm sel})^{N_{\tau}}. The binomial CDF increases with the wrong count, so zero errors minimize the p-value at fixed NτN_{\tau}; issuance requires

Nτ≥⌈log⁡(δ/M)log⁡(1−αsel)⌉.N_{\tau}\geq\left\lceil\frac{\log(\delta/M)}{\log(1-\alpha_{\rm sel})}\right\rceil.

With M=10,δ=0.1M=10,\delta=0.1, the necessary accepted counts at conditional-error targets 10%, 15%, 20%, and 30% are respectively 44, 29, 21, and 13. These are necessary volume conditions, not a guarantee of issuance. The family-wise guarantee covers one declared model–domain–budget and error-target configuration; reporting multiple configurations gives no joint guarantee across them.

A.4 Proofs and scope of Proposition 1

A.4.1 Group advantages and mixed failures

Write μλ=pR−λ​pW\mu_{\lambda}=p_{R}-\lambda p_{W} for the expected reward. Condition on the first trajectory. Independence of the remaining G−1G-1 rollouts gives

𝔼⁡[A1∣Y1=y]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[A_{1}\mid Y_{1}=y] =rλ​(y)−rλ​(y)+(G−1)​μλG\displaystyle=r_{\lambda}(y)-\frac{r_{\lambda}(y)+(G-1)\mu_{\lambda}}{G}
=γG​{rλ​(y)−μλ}.\displaystyle=\gamma_{G}\{r_{\lambda}(y)-\mu_{\lambda}\}.

Substituting rλ​(R)=1r_{\lambda}(R)=1, rλ​(W)=−λr_{\lambda}(W)=-\lambda, and rλ​(U)=0r_{\lambda}(U)=0 proves (5). Conditional statements are understood only for outcomes having positive probability. If pR+pW>0p_{R}+p_{W}>0, then

λ​pW−pR>0⟺(1+λ)​pR<λ⁡(pR+pW)⟺pRpR+pW<λ1+λ.\lambda p_{W}-p_{R}>0\ \Longleftrightarrow\ (1+\lambda)p_{R}<\lambda(p_{R}+p_{W})\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \frac{p_{R}}{p_{R}+p_{W}}<\frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda}.

If pR=pW=0p_{R}=p_{W}=0, all rewards and advantages are zero and the precision ratio is undefined, so no phase-transition claim is needed. For an actual group with counts (NR,NW,NU)(N_{R},N_{W},N_{U}), every UU rollout has

AU=λ​NW−NRG.A_{U}=\frac{\lambda N_{W}-N_{R}}{G}.

At λ=0\lambda=0, this is nonpositive in every group, strengthening the conditional-expectation statement. Sampled RR advantages are always nonnegative, and sampled WW advantages are always nonpositive.

Reward-varying groups.

For λ=0\lambda=0, a group has a nonconstant reward vector exactly when it contains both an RR and a non-RR. Its probability is

1−pRG−(1−pR)G.1-p_{R}^{G}-(1-p_{R})^{G}.

For λ>0\lambda>0, the three outcome classes have distinct rewards, so the corresponding probability is 1−pRG−pWG−pUG1-p_{R}^{G}-p_{W}^{G}-p_{U}^{G}. Subtracting proves (6). Equivalently, the additional event is {NR=0,NW>0,NU>0}\{N_{R}=0,N_{W}>0,N_{U}>0\}, on which AU=λ​NW/G>0A_{U}=\lambda N_{W}/G>0 and AW=−λNU/G<0A_{W}=-\lambda N_{U}/G<0. The phrase reward-varying does not assert that an arbitrary shared parameterization must have a nonzero parameter gradient on that group.

A.4.2 Positive non-submission rewards: proof of Corollary A.1

Corollary A.1 (A common non-submission reward raises the effective penalty).

If r⁡(R)=1r(R)=1, r⁡(W)=−λr(W)=-\lambda, and r⁡(U)=ρr(U)=\rho with λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 and 0≤ρ<10\leq\rho<1, the group advantages satisfy

Agλ,ρ=(1−ρ)​Agλeff,0,λeff=λ+ρ1−ρ.A_{g}^{\lambda,\rho}=(1-\rho)A_{g}^{\lambda_{\rm eff},0},\qquad\lambda_{\rm eff}=\frac{\lambda+\rho}{1-\rho}. (A.3)

The break-even submitted-answer precision becomes (λ+ρ)/(1+λ)(\lambda+\rho)/(1+\lambda).

Proof. The conditional calculation and affine reward identity are as follows.

Let rλ,ρ​(R)=1r_{\lambda,\rho}(R)=1, rλ,ρ​(W)=−λr_{\lambda,\rho}(W)=-\lambda, and rλ,ρ​(U)=ρr_{\lambda,\rho}(U)=\rho, with λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 and 0≤ρ<10\leq\rho<1. For the same independent group of G≥2G\geq 2 rollouts, write γG=(G−1)/G\gamma_{G}=(G-1)/G. Conditioning as in Proposition 1 gives, whenever pU>0p_{U}>0,

𝔼⁡[A1∣U]=γG​{ρ⁡(pR+pW)+λ​pW−pR}.\mathbb{E}[A_{1}\mid U]=\gamma_{G}\{\rho(p_{R}+p_{W})+\lambda p_{W}-p_{R}\}. (A.4)

Indeed, the mean reward is μλ,ρ=pR−λ​pW+ρ​pU\mu_{\lambda,\rho}=p_{R}-\lambda p_{W}+\rho p_{U} and the conditional advantage is γG​(ρ−μλ,ρ)\gamma_{G}(\rho-\mu_{\lambda,\rho}). For pR+pW>0p_{R}+p_{W}>0, its sign is positive exactly when

pRpR+pW<λ+ρ1+λ.\frac{p_{R}}{p_{R}+p_{W}}<\frac{\lambda+\rho}{1+\lambda}. (A.5)

If pR=pW=0p_{R}=p_{W}=0, every group reward equals ρ\rho and every advantage is zero.

The affine transformation

r′=rλ,ρ−ρ1−ρ=(1,−λeff,0),λeff=λ+ρ1−ρ,r^{\prime}=\frac{r_{\lambda,\rho}-\rho}{1-\rho}=\left(1,-\lambda_{\mathrm{eff}},0\right),\qquad\lambda_{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{\lambda+\rho}{1-\rho},

has an exact groupwise consequence: Agλ,ρ=(1−ρ)​Agλeff,0A_{g}^{\lambda,\rho}=(1-\rho)A_{g}^{\lambda_{\mathrm{eff}},0}. The additive constant cancels in group centering, and the positive rescaling multiplies the raw advantage-weighted gradient by 1−ρ1-\rho. This is an identity of rewards, advantages, and the corresponding raw surrogate gradient; it does not identify a shared neural policy’s trajectory under AdamW, gradient clipping, or additional loss terms. The restriction ρ<1\rho<1 ensures a positive scaling and keeps a correct answer strictly preferable to non-submission. At ρ=1\rho=1, those outcomes tie and this reduction is undefined.

In the specified attempt–solver model, the objective becomes

Jλ,ρ​(a,q)=ρ+a⁡{(1+λ)​q−λ−ρ}.J_{\lambda,\rho}(a,q)=\rho+a\{(1+\lambda)q-\lambda-\rho\}.

With the same product Bernoulli mirror metric, the exact flow is

a˙=a⁡(1−a)​{(1+λ)​q−λ−ρ},q˙=κ⁡(1+λ)​a​q​(1−q).\dot{a}=a(1-a)\{(1+\lambda)q-\lambda-\rho\},\qquad\dot{q}=\kappa(1+\lambda)aq(1-q).

For λ+ρ>0\lambda+\rho>0, put qc=(λ+ρ)/(1+λ)∈(0,1)q_{c}=(\lambda+\rho)/(1+\lambda)\in(0,1). The invariant −qc​log⁡q−(1−qc)​log⁡(1−q)+κ​log⁡(1−a)-q_{c}\log q-(1-q_{c})\log(1-q)+\kappa\log(1-a) is unchanged in form. Consequently, for a0,q0∈(0,1)a_{0},q_{0}\in(0,1) with q0<qcq_{0}<q_{c}, the exact starvation criterion remains

DBer(qc∥q0)≥−κlog(1−a0).D_{\mathrm{Ber}}(q_{c}\|q_{0})\geq-\kappa\log(1-a_{0}).

The same proof gives (a,q)→(0,q∞)(a,q)\to(0,q_{\infty}) with q∞≤qcq_{\infty}\leq q_{c} under this inequality, and recovery to (1,1)(1,1) under the reverse strict inequality; q0≥qcq_{0}\geq q_{c} also gives recovery. Thus a common positive non-submission reward raises break-even precision even without an explicit wrong-answer penalty: at λ=0\lambda=0, qc=ρq_{c}=\rho.

Rewarding only explicit refusal is a different four-outcome intervention. For rewards (1,−λ,ρA,0)(1,-\lambda,\rho_{A},0) on (R,W,UA,UT)(R,W,U_{A},U_{T}), where UAU_{A} is explicit refusal and UTU_{T} is truncation, the common-UU reduction above does not apply. In particular, when both subtypes have positive probability,

𝔼⁡[A1∣UA]−𝔼⁡[A1∣UT]=γG​ρA.\mathbb{E}[A_{1}\mid U_{A}]-\mathbb{E}[A_{1}\mid U_{T}]=\gamma_{G}\rho_{A}.

Positive ρA\rho_{A} breaks their reward tie and expressly favors refusal over truncation at the reward level. It does not by itself specify probability flow or a deployment marginal-risk guarantee. These positive-reward shaping variants were not evaluated in the experiments.

A.4.3 Gradient identity and policy parameterization

Group-centered policy gradients also admit a U-statistic interpretation [39]. The direct covariance derivation below isolates the effect of the ternary reward and applies to arbitrary rollout features. Exchangeability within the group gives 𝔼⁡[G−1​∑gAg​ψg]=𝔼⁡[A1​ψ1]\mathbb{E}[G^{-1}\sum_{g}A_{g}\psi_{g}]=\mathbb{E}[A_{1}\psi_{1}]. Using independence for j≠1j\neq 1,

𝔼⁡[A1​ψ1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[A_{1}\psi_{1}] =𝔼⁡[r1​ψ1]−1G​𝔼​[r1​ψ1]−1G​∑j=2G𝔼⁡[rj]​𝔼​[ψ1]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[r_{1}\psi_{1}]-\frac{1}{G}\mathbb{E}[r_{1}\psi_{1}]-\frac{1}{G}\sum_{j=2}^{G}\mathbb{E}[r_{j}]\mathbb{E}[\psi_{1}]
=γG​{𝔼⁡[rλ​ψ]−𝔼⁡[rλ]​𝔼​[ψ]}.\displaystyle=\gamma_{G}\{\mathbb{E}[r_{\lambda}\psi]-\mathbb{E}[r_{\lambda}]\mathbb{E}[\psi]\}.

Here ψ\psi need not be a score function. If QθQ_{\theta} has a differentiable density on a locally fixed support, rewards have no direct dependence on θ\theta, and differentiation can be interchanged with integration, then

𝔼Qθ​∇θ​log⁡Qθ=0,∇θ𝔼Qθ​rλ=𝔼Qθ​[rλ​∇θ​log⁡Qθ],\mathbb{E}_{Q_{\theta}}\nabla_{\theta}\log Q_{\theta}=0,\qquad\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{Q_{\theta}}r_{\lambda}=\mathbb{E}_{Q_{\theta}}[r_{\lambda}\nabla_{\theta}\log Q_{\theta}],

which proves the score-function specialization.

Connection to the implemented surrogate.

Fix token denominator G​BGB and mask deterministic environment tokens. The unclipped token-ratio surrogate’s gradient at the behavior-policy point is

g^=1G​B​∑g=1GAg​∑t∈𝒯gsampled∇θ​log​πθ​(yg,t∣hg,t).\widehat{g}=\frac{1}{GB}\sum_{g=1}^{G}A_{g}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{g}^{\mathrm{sampled}}}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{g,t}\mid h_{g,t}).

Thus (7) applies to the summed token feature with the constant 1/B1/B. Fixed BB prevents per-trajectory length weighting. Deterministic prefills, injected end-of-thinking tokens, and forced stopping are unsampled and contribute no score term.

The experiments use top-pp and top-kk sampling. If the optimized log-probability is that of the raw model πθ\pi_{\theta}, while trajectories come from a transformed law QθQ_{\theta}, the exact statement is the covariance identity, not automatically ∇θ𝔼Qθ​rλ\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{Q_{\theta}}r_{\lambda}. On a region with a fixed truncation set 𝒱⁡(h)\mathcal{V}(h), for example, qθ(v∣h)=πθ(v∣h)𝟏{v∈𝒱(h)}/Zθ(h)q_{\theta}(v\mid h)=\pi_{\theta}(v\mid h)\mathbf{1}\{v\in\mathcal{V}(h)\}/Z_{\theta}(h) has score ∇log⁡qθ=∇log⁡πθ−∇log⁡Zθ\nabla\log q_{\theta}=\nabla\log\pi_{\theta}-\nabla\log Z_{\theta}. Prefix-dependent normalizer terms generally persist in the reward covariance; changing truncation sets require separate analysis.

For standard positive-width PPO clipping, ratios equal to one lie in the unclipped region, so the behavior-point derivative agrees with the unclipped derivative above. This does not identify later clipped inner-loop derivatives. AdamW, gradient clipping, parameter sharing, and finite stochastic updates also prevent equating the raw expected gradient with the trained LLM’s exact probability flow.

Why the sign of a conditional advantage is not a universal drift theorem.

For diagnostic purposes, consider a terminal three-action softmax with logits ziz_{i}, and rescale time to absorb γG/B\gamma_{G}/B. Exact Euclidean gradient ascent on J=pR−λ​pWJ=p_{R}-\lambda p_{W} has

z˙i=pi​{ri−μλ}.\dot{z}_{i}=p_{i}\{r_{i}-\mu_{\lambda}\}.

Writing S2=pR2+pW2+pU2S_{2}=p_{R}^{2}+p_{W}^{2}+p_{U}^{2} and differentiating pRp_{R} gives

p˙R=pR2​(1−2​pR+S2)−λ​pR​pW​(S2−pR−pW).\dot{p}_{R}=p_{R}^{2}(1-2p_{R}+S_{2})-\lambda p_{R}p_{W}(S_{2}-p_{R}-p_{W}). (A.6)

p˙i=pi​(ri−μλ),pi​(t)=pi​(0)​eri​t∑jpj​(0)​erj​t.\dot{p}_{i}=p_{i}(r_{i}-\mu_{\lambda}),\qquad p_{i}(t)=\frac{p_{i}(0)e^{r_{i}t}}{\sum_{j}p_{j}(0)e^{r_{j}t}}. (A.7)

pRλ​(t)=pR​(0)​etpR​(0)​et+pU​(0)+pW​(0)​e−λ​t≥pR0​(t).p_{R}^{\lambda}(t)=\frac{p_{R}(0)e^{t}}{p_{R}(0)e^{t}+p_{U}(0)+p_{W}(0)e^{-\lambda t}}\geq p_{R}^{0}(t).

Thus reward ordering alone implies neither a universal all-UU attractor nor universal frontier contraction.

A.4.4 An attempt–solver model with a sharp starvation boundary

We now exhibit assumptions under which a genuine boundary attractor can occur, rather than attributing one to Dr. GRPO without a dynamics model. A gate attempts a solution with probability a∈(0,1)a\in(0,1); conditional success probability is q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1). Otherwise it produces UU. Then

pR=a​q,pW=a⁡(1−q),pU=1−a,Jλ​(a,q)=a⁡{(1+λ)​q−λ}.p_{R}=aq,\quad p_{W}=a(1-q),\quad p_{U}=1-a,\qquad J_{\lambda}(a,q)=a\{(1+\lambda)q-\lambda\}.

Use the product Bernoulli mirror metric, with relative solver learning rate κ>0\kappa>0:

M⁡(a,q)=diag⁡(1a⁡(1−a),1κ​q​(1−q)).M(a,q)=\operatorname{diag}\left(\frac{1}{a(1-a)},\,\frac{1}{\kappa q(1-q)}\right).

This is a specified block mirror-flow model. In particular, its metric is not the Fisher information metric of the full gated trajectory law: the latter contains an extra visitation factor aa in the solver block. The factor aa remaining in q˙\dot{q} represents learning that slows when solution attempts become rare.

For λ>0\lambda>0, write qc=λ/(1+λ)q_{c}=\lambda/(1+\lambda) and suppose q0<qcq_{0}<q_{c}. Let

{a(t)→0,q(t)→q∞≤qc,DBer(qc∥q0)≥−κlog(1−a0),a(t)→1,q(t)→1,DBer(qc∥q0)<−κlog(1−a0).\begin{cases}a(t)\to 0,\ q(t)\to q_{\infty}\leq q_{c},&D_{\mathrm{Ber}}(q_{c}\|q_{0})\geq-\kappa\log(1-a_{0}),\\ a(t)\to 1,\ q(t)\to 1,&D_{\mathrm{Ber}}(q_{c}\|q_{0})<-\kappa\log(1-a_{0}).\end{cases} (A.9)

A.5 Proofs and scope of Proposition A.1

Proposition A.1 (Deployment-dependent selection and reward-equivalent abstention).

For a frozen candidate generator, let η⁡(z)=P⁡(R∣z,valid)\eta(z)=P(R\mid z,\mathrm{valid}) be posterior correctness from selector information zz. For α>0\alpha>0, maximizing correct submissions with W≤αW\leq\alpha over randomized selectors measurable in zz gives

g⋆(z)=𝕀{η(z)>λ⋆/(1+λ⋆)},g^{\star}(z)=\mathbb{I}\{\eta(z)>\lambda^{\star}/(1+\lambda^{\star})\}, (A.12)

with possible randomization at equality. The optimal dual multiplier depends in general on both α\alpha and the deployment population, including when η⁡(z)\eta(z) is unchanged under shift. If explicit abstention and truncation both receive zero reward, redistributing probability between them at fixed (pR,pW)(p_{R},p_{W}) leaves the objective unchanged; their conditional expected advantages are identical.

Proof. We derive the optimal selector, exhibit its population dependence, and verify reward equivalence.

Bayes rule and ties.

Let νP\nu_{P} be the subprobability law of valid candidates and their selector information, so νP​(𝒵)=P​(valid)\nu_{P}(\mathcal{Z})=P(\mathrm{valid}). For a randomized selector g:𝒵→[0,1]g\colon\mathcal{Z}\to[0,1], write RP​(g)=∫g​η​d​νPR_{P}(g)=\int g\eta\,d\nu_{P} and WP​(g)=∫g⁡(1−η)​d​νPW_{P}(g)=\int g(1-\eta)\,d\nu_{P}. Assume α>0\alpha>0. For λ≥0\lambda\geq 0, the Lagrangian is

ℒ⁡(g,λ)=λ​α+∫g⁡(z)​{η⁡(z)−λ⁡(1−η⁡(z))}​d​νP​(z).{\cal L}(g,\lambda)=\lambda\alpha+\int g(z)\{\eta(z)-\lambda(1-\eta(z))\}\,d\nu_{P}(z).

Pointwise maximization over g⁡(z)∈[0,1]g(z)\in[0,1] gives (A.12); at zero coefficient any value in [0,1][0,1] is optimal. Retaining the constant term, the resulting dual objective is

dP​(λ)=λ​α+∫{η−λ⁡(1−η)}+​d​νP.d_{P}(\lambda)=\lambda\alpha+\int\{\eta-\lambda(1-\eta)\}_{+}\,d\nu_{P}.

It is continuous and convex, and dP​(λ)≥λ​αd_{P}(\lambda)\geq\lambda\alpha, so it attains a finite minimum for α>0\alpha>0. At an interior minimizer, the subgradient condition permits a randomization on the equality set making WP​(g⋆)=αW_{P}(g^{\star})=\alpha. At λ⋆=0\lambda^{\star}=0, one can choose a maximizer with WP​(g⋆)≤αW_{P}(g^{\star})\leq\alpha. Equivalently, order points by the posterior odds η/(1−η)\eta/(1-\eta) under the wrong-mass measure (1−η)​d​νP(1-\eta)d\nu_{P} and fill up to a budget of mass α\alpha, randomizing at a boundary atom. Points with η=1\eta=1 are accepted at no wrong-answer cost.

For completeness, any feasible gg and the resulting g⋆g^{\star} satisfy

RP​(g)−RP​(g⋆)\displaystyle R_{P}(g)-R_{P}(g^{\star}) =∫(g−g⋆)​{η−λ⋆​(1−η)}​d​νP\displaystyle=\int(g-g^{\star})\{\eta-\lambda^{\star}(1-\eta)\}\,d\nu_{P}
+λ⋆​{WP​(g)−WP​(g⋆)}≤0.\displaystyle\quad+\lambda^{\star}\{W_{P}(g)-W_{P}(g^{\star})\}\leq 0.

The first term is nonpositive by pointwise maximization; the second is nonpositive by feasibility and complementary slackness. This proves optimality directly. If the budget exceeds the raw wrong-answer mass, accepting all valid candidates is optimal and λ=0\lambda=0 suffices. At α=0\alpha=0, accepting only posterior-certain correct candidates is optimal, and a finite dual threshold need not exist.

A concrete distribution-shift counterexample.

Let all candidates be valid, let Z∈[0,1]Z\in[0,1], and let correctness conditional on Z=zZ=z be Bernoulli with probability η⁡(z)=z\eta(z)=z. On the source population Z∼Unif⁡[0,1]Z\sim\mathrm{Unif}[0,1], a cutoff tt has

Wsrc​(t)=∫t1(1−z)​𝑑z=(1−t)22.W_{\mathrm{src}}(t)=\int_{t}^{1}(1-z)\,dz=\frac{(1-t)^{2}}{2}.

For α=0.02\alpha=0.02, the unique cutoff is t=0.8t=0.8 and λsrc⋆=4\lambda^{\star}_{\mathrm{src}}=4. Now shift only the feature distribution to Z∼Unif⁡[0.5,1]Z\sim\mathrm{Unif}[0.5,1], retaining the identical correctness function η⁡(z)=z\eta(z)=z. The same threshold has

Wtgt​(0.8)=2​∫0.81(1−z)​𝑑z=0.04.W_{\mathrm{tgt}}(0.8)=2\int_{0.8}^{1}(1-z)\,dz=0.04.

The target-optimal threshold is ttgt⋆=1−0.02t^{\star}_{\mathrm{tgt}}=1-\sqrt{0.02} and λtgt⋆=1/0.02−1≈6.0711\lambda^{\star}_{\mathrm{tgt}}=1/\sqrt{0.02}-1\approx 6.0711. Even this shift toward easier candidates doubles the marginal wrong rate of the fixed rule because it changes accepted population mass. The source optimum also depends on the risk target: λ⋆​(α)=1/2​α−1\lambda^{\star}(\alpha)=1/\sqrt{2\alpha}-1 for 0<α<1/20<\alpha<1/2.

This is non-transferability of the optimal operating point in general, not a claim that every shift changes the optimum or that no fixed penalty can ever be conservative. Under an oracle posterior threshold,

WP​(gλ)≤ℙ⁡(accepted)1+λ≤11+λ.W_{P}(g_{\lambda})\leq\frac{\mathbb{P}(\mathrm{accepted})}{1+\lambda}\leq\frac{1}{1+\lambda}.

Thus λ≥α−1−1\lambda\geq\alpha^{-1}-1 is a distribution-uniform sufficient choice in this ideal Bayes problem, often at a substantial coverage cost. The bound is sharp in the supremum over populations by concentrating mass just above the acceptance threshold. A trained neural penalty policy is not assumed to implement an oracle posterior threshold. None of these facts requires full solver retraining: changing a post-hoc selector changes its operating point with weights held fixed.

Reward degeneracy and the role of geometry.

With (R,W,UA,UT)(R,W,U_{A},U_{T}) rewards (1,−λ,0,0)(1,-\lambda,0,0), J=pR−λ​pWJ=p_{R}-\lambda p_{W} does not contain pAp_{A} or pTp_{T} separately. Hence the feasible perturbation (pA,pT)↦(pA+ε,pT−ε)(p_{A},p_{T})\mapsto(p_{A}+\varepsilon,p_{T}-\varepsilon) has zero directional derivative. Conditioning as above gives 𝔼⁡[A∣UA]=𝔼⁡[A∣UT]=−γG​μλ\mathbb{E}[A\mid U_{A}]=\mathbb{E}[A\mid U_{T}]=-\gamma_{G}\mu_{\lambda}.

In the full-simplex replicator geometry, p˙A=−μλ​pA\dot{p}_{A}=-\mu_{\lambda}p_{A} and p˙T=−μλ​pT\dot{p}_{T}=-\mu_{\lambda}p_{T}, so

dd​t​log⁡pApT=0.\frac{d}{dt}\log\frac{p_{A}}{p_{T}}=0.

Their odds preserve their initialization; when both derivatives are nonzero, their absolute flow ratio equals pA/pTp_{A}/p_{T}. Euclidean ascent in independent outcome logits has z˙A=−μλ​pA\dot{z}_{A}=-\mu_{\lambda}p_{A} and z˙T=−μλ​pT\dot{z}_{T}=-\mu_{\lambda}p_{T}, giving

dd​t​log⁡pApT=−μλ​(pA−pT).\frac{d}{dt}\log\frac{p_{A}}{p_{T}}=-\mu_{\lambda}(p_{A}-p_{T}).

Thus even two standard geometries give different relative flows. Shared neural parameters or Adam preconditioning can give still different behavior. A reward preference for explicit abstention over truncation would break the tie, but alone gives no deployment marginal-risk guarantee.

What can be proved about frontier contraction.

For any frozen generator and any selector, RP​(g)≤ℙP​(Y=R)R_{P}(g)\leq\mathbb{P}_{P}(Y=R): filtering cannot create a correct candidate. Sharper set inclusion holds under an explicit thinning assumption. Suppose a second generator preserves the original candidate and its selector information but retains it with probability h⁡(Z)∈[0,1]h(Z)\in[0,1], independently of correctness conditional on ZZ; otherwise it returns UU. Its valid-candidate law is h​d​νPh\,d\nu_{P}. Any selector gg on the thinned generator attains

(R,W)=(∫h​g​η​d​νP,∫h​g​(1−η)​d​νP),(R,W)=\left(\int hg\eta\,d\nu_{P},\;\int hg(1-\eta)\,d\nu_{P}\right),

which the original generator attains using the randomized selector h​ghg. Its attainable set of (R,W)(R,W) pairs is therefore a subset of the original generator’s attainable set.

With valid coverage aa and fixed correctness probability q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1), the attempt model gives

maxg:W⁡(g)≤αR(g)=qmin{a,α1−q}.\max_{g:\,W(g)\leq\alpha}R(g)=q\min\left\{a,\frac{\alpha}{1-q}\right\}.

Reducing aa can strictly reduce the frontier once the smaller candidate supply binds, while sufficiently tight risk budgets give the same optimum. This is a sufficient condition for contraction, not a theorem that arbitrary penalty training is such a thinning. Training can alter both candidate quality and the score distribution. Indeed, (A.7) gives a counterexample to any universal contraction assertion: increasing λ\lambda there raises pR​(t)p_{R}(t) and lowers pW​(t)p_{W}(t) from the same initial state.

A.6 Score anatomy: complete proofs and boundaries

A.6.1 Length and discrimination

In a continuous length-factor surrogate with independent Gaussian log factors, suppose 𝔼⁡D=d\E D=d, 𝔼⁡Bℓ=b\E B_{\ell}=b and variances vD,vB>0v_{D},v_{B}>0. Writing Φ\Phi for the standard normal cumulative distribution function,

AUC⁡(Ssum)=Φ⁡(d−bvD+vB).\operatorname{AUC}(S_{\rm sum})=\Phi\!\left(\frac{d-b}{\sqrt{v_{D}+v_{B}}}\right). (A.13)

Even if d>0d>0, the ranking reverses when b>db>d.

For the general Gaussian extension, use B=BℓB=B_{\ell} from Proposition 2. In a stylized positive-factor model, now allowing LL to be real valued, suppose the within-class vectors (log⁡Ly,log⁡ℓ¯y)(\log L_{y},\log\bar{\ell}_{y}) are jointly Gaussian. Define d=𝔼​log⁡ℓ¯W−𝔼​log⁡ℓ¯Rd=\mathbb{E}\log\bar{\ell}_{W}-\mathbb{E}\log\bar{\ell}_{R}, b=𝔼​log⁡LR−𝔼​log⁡LWb=\mathbb{E}\log L_{R}-\mathbb{E}\log L_{W}, vU=∑y∈{R,W}Var⁡(log⁡ℓ¯y)v_{U}=\sum_{y\in\{R,W\}}\operatorname{Var}(\log\bar{\ell}_{y}), vL=∑yVar⁡(log⁡Ly)v_{L}=\sum_{y}\operatorname{Var}(\log L_{y}), and c=∑yCov⁡(log⁡Ly,log⁡ℓ¯y)c=\sum_{y}\operatorname{Cov}(\log L_{y},\log\bar{\ell}_{y}). For vU>0v_{U}>0 and vU+vL+2​c>0v_{U}+v_{L}+2c>0,

AUC⁡(ℓ¯)=Φ⁡(dvU),AUC⁡(Ssum)=Φ⁡(d−bvU+vL+2​c).\operatorname{AUC}(\bar{\ell})=\Phi\!\left(\frac{d}{\sqrt{v_{U}}}\right),\qquad\operatorname{AUC}(S_{\rm sum})=\Phi\!\left(\frac{d-b}{\sqrt{v_{U}+v_{L}+2c}}\right). (A.14)

When c=0c=0, the independent-factor specialization uses vD=vUv_{D}=v_{U} and vB=vLv_{B}=v_{L}. Consequently the summed score reverses direction exactly when b>db>d in this model. If d>0d>0, b≥0b\geq 0, and the two log factors are independent within each class, length strictly reduces AUROC whenever b>0b>0 or vL>0v_{L}>0.

Proof of Proposition 2 and its Gaussian extension.

The factorization follows directly from the definition of the arithmetic mean. Since the logarithm is strictly increasing on (0,∞)(0,\infty),

LWℓ¯W>LRℓ¯R⟺logℓ¯W−logℓ¯R>logLR−logLW.L_{W}\bar{\ell}_{W}>L_{R}\bar{\ell}_{R}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\log\bar{\ell}_{W}-\log\bar{\ell}_{R}>\log L_{R}-\log L_{W}.

The same equivalence holds with equality. Multiplying the strict-event probability by one and the tie-event probability by one half proves (10). If a span has zero average surprise, omit only the logarithmic reparameterization; the product identity and original AUROC definition remain valid.

For the Gaussian model, independence of the two class draws and the stated within-class joint normality imply that DD is normal with mean dd and variance vUv_{U}. Also,

D−B=(log⁡LW+log⁡ℓ¯W)−(log⁡LR+log⁡ℓ¯R)D-B=(\log L_{W}+\log\bar{\ell}_{W})-(\log L_{R}+\log\bar{\ell}_{R})

is normal with mean d−bd-b and variance vU+vL+2​cv_{U}+v_{L}+2c. A normal random variable with mean mm and positive standard deviation ss exceeds zero with probability Φ⁡(m/s)\Phi(m/s) and has no atom at zero. This proves (A.14). Since Φ\Phi is strictly increasing and Φ⁡(0)=1/2\Phi(0)=1/2, the summed score has AUROC below 1/21/2 exactly when d−b<0d-b<0. If the factors are independent within each class, c=0c=0. When d>0d>0 and b≥0b\geq 0, either d−b≤0d-b\leq 0, in which case the comparison with d/vU>0d/\sqrt{v_{U}}>0 is immediate, or

d−bvU+vL≤dvU,\frac{d-b}{\sqrt{v_{U}+v_{L}}}\leq\frac{d}{\sqrt{v_{U}}},

with strict inequality when b>0b>0 or vL>0v_{L}>0. This proves the stated degradation claim. With a zero Gaussian variance, the corresponding score gap is deterministic and its AUROC is ψ\psi of its mean; this also describes the degenerate boundaries omitted from the displayed positive-variance formula. ∎

An exact accounting of the direction changes is useful. If Pr⁡(D=0)=Pr⁡(D=B)=0\Pr(D=0)=\Pr(D=B)=0, then

AUC⁡(Ssum)−AUC⁡(ℓ¯)=Pr⁡(B<D≤0)−Pr⁡(0<D≤B).\operatorname{AUC}(S_{\rm sum})-\operatorname{AUC}(\bar{\ell})=\Pr(B<D\leq 0)-\Pr(0<D\leq B). (A.15)

Subtracting the indicators gives +1+1 only when an incorrect ordering becomes correct, and −1-1 only for the reverse change. Without the no-ties condition one simply uses 𝔼⁡[ψ⁡(D−B)−ψ⁡(D)]\mathbb{E}[\psi(D-B)-\psi(D)], which is exact for all distributions. A direct sufficient condition for non-increasing AUROC is B≥0B\geq 0 almost surely for the independent right–wrong pair, because ψ\psi is nondecreasing. Marginal stochastic dominance of lengths is substantially weaker than this pairwise condition.

Why stochastic dominance is insufficient.

Let a right draw equal (LR,ℓ¯R)=(2,1)(L_{R},\bar{\ell}_{R})=(2,1) with probability 0.80.8 and (4,4)(4,4) with probability 0.20.2. Let an independent wrong draw equal (1,3)(1,3) with probability 0.80.8 and (3,0.8)(3,0.8) with probability 0.20.2. The right length stochastically dominates the wrong length: its quantiles exceed the latter’s by one. The mean-score AUROC is 0.8⋅0.8=0.640.8\cdot 0.8=0.64. The summed scores are 22 or 1616 on right draws and 33 or 2.42.4 on wrong draws, giving AUROC 0.80.8. Hence even strict length dominance and positive mean-score discrimination can coexist with an improvement after summation. Dependence between length and token surprise matters.

Why a median comparison is insufficient.

Let LW=1L_{W}=1, LR=1L_{R}=1 with probability 0.490.49 and LR=2L_{R}=2 otherwise. Let ℓ¯R=1\bar{\ell}_{R}=1, and independently set log⁡ℓ¯W=0.1\log\bar{\ell}_{W}=0.1 with probability 0.510.51 and 11 otherwise. Then the unique median of BB is log⁡2\log 2, exceeding the unique median 0.10.1 of DD, whereas

AUC⁡(Ssum)=0.49+0.51⋅0.49=0.7399>12.\operatorname{AUC}(S_{\rm sum})=0.49+0.51\cdot 0.49=0.7399>\tfrac{1}{2}.

The mean score has AUROC one. Means alone are insufficient under arbitrary sub-Gaussian assumptions: take B=log⁡2B=\log 2 and independently D=1D=1 with probability 0.510.51 and D=0.1D=0.1 otherwise. Both variables are bounded and therefore sub-Gaussian, 𝔼​D=0.559<log⁡2\mathbb{E}D=0.559<\log 2, but Pr⁡(D>B)=0.51\Pr(D>B)=0.51. The Gaussian sign-reversal criterion requires normality or another restriction on the full centered contrast distribution.

A.6.2 Finite empirical CVaR, rounding, and replication

Primal and dual identities in Proposition 3.

For every η\eta and every kk-element subset JJ,
