The bound is attained when coordinate ii already belongs to a strictly separated top-kk set. Setting k=1k=1 gives the maximum’s sharp bound. ∎

Lemma A.1 (Exact rounding error and replication bound).

Let 0<β≤10<\beta\leq 1, a=β​La=\beta L, k=⌈a⌉k=\lceil a\rceil, and r=k−ar=k-a. Denote fixed-tail-mass empirical CVaR by

Cβ​(z)=minη⁡{η+1β​L​∑t=1L(zt−η)+}.C_{\beta}(z)=\min_{\eta}\left\{\eta+\frac{1}{\beta L}\sum_{t=1}^{L}(z_{t}-\eta)_{+}\right\}.

Then

Cβ​(z)−Tk​(z)=ra​(Tk​(z)−z(k))=rk​(Cβ​(z)−z(k)),C_{\beta}(z)-T_{k}(z)=\frac{r}{a}\bigl(T_{k}(z)-z_{(k)}\bigr)=\frac{r}{k}\bigl(C_{\beta}(z)-z_{(k)}\bigr), (A.16)

and, with range⁡(z)=z(1)−z(L)\operatorname{range}(z)=z_{(1)}-z_{(L)},

0≤Cβ​(z)−Tk​(z)≤k−β​Lk​range⁡(z).0\leq C_{\beta}(z)-T_{k}(z)\leq\frac{k-\beta L}{k}\operatorname{range}(z).

If z[c]z^{[c]} repeats each coordinate cc times, for an integer c≥1c\geq 1, then

0≤T⌈β​c​L⌉​(z[c])−Tk​(z)≤k−β​Lk​range⁡(z).0\leq T_{\lceil\beta cL\rceil}(z^{[c]})-T_{k}(z)\leq\frac{k-\beta L}{k}\operatorname{range}(z). (A.17)

Fixed-β\beta CVaR is exactly replication-invariant. The rounded score is exactly replication-invariant whenever β​L\beta L is integral; it need not be so otherwise.

Proof.

For noninteger aa, write a=m+θa=m+\theta, where m=⌊a⌋m=\lfloor a\rfloor and θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1). Evaluating the piecewise-linear objective at η=z(m+1)\eta=z_{(m+1)} gives

Cβ​(z)=∑j=1mz(j)+θ​z(m+1)a.C_{\beta}(z)=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{m}z_{(j)}+\theta z_{(m+1)}}{a}.

To see that this is minimal, observe that on each interval between successive ordered coordinates the derivative is 1−j/a1-j/a, where jj coordinates exceed η\eta; the slope changes from nonpositive to nonnegative at this quantile. Ties give the same value. For integer aa, the analogous value is the average of the first aa coordinates. Thus in both cases

a​Cβ​(z)=k​Tk​(z)−r​z(k).aC_{\beta}(z)=kT_{k}(z)-rz_{(k)}.

Rearrangement yields both identities in (A.16). Because z(k)≤Cβ​(z)≤z(1)z_{(k)}\leq C_{\beta}(z)\leq z_{(1)}, their common value is nonnegative and at most r​range⁡(z)/kr\operatorname{range}(z)/k.

Repeating coordinates preserves their empirical probability measure, so the fixed-β\beta CVaR objective and its value are unchanged. Moreover

β≤⌈c​β​L⌉c​L≤⌈β​L⌉L.\beta\leq\frac{\lceil c\beta L\rceil}{cL}\leq\frac{\lceil\beta L\rceil}{L}.

An upper-tail average is nonincreasing in its tail mass. This follows directly by adding lower quantile values to the averaged upper portion, or from the dual representation. It follows that

Tk​(z)≤T⌈c​β​L⌉​(z[c])≤Cβ​(z).T_{k}(z)\leq T_{\lceil c\beta L\rceil}(z^{[c]})\leq C_{\beta}(z).

Combine this with the rounding bound. For integral aa, both endpoints coincide, giving exact invariance. ∎

For example, with β=0.1\beta=0.1, L=11L=11, one coordinate equal to one and the other ten equal to zero, the implemented score is 1/21/2. Repeating each coordinate ten times gives a score 10/1110/11. Thus the rounded score removes linear growth with replication but is not exactly replication-invariant for short spans. The bound is pathwise: an absolute small-error conclusion additionally requires control of the realized score range. NLL has no universal finite upper bound. Replication also does not model an arbitrary change of tokenization, which can change the empirical surprise distribution itself.

A.6.3 Sparse signal, background noise, and selective submission

For an explanatory model, fix LL and a set CC of kk critical positions. Conditional on class y∈{0,1}y\in\{0,1\}, with 0=R0=R and 1=W1=W, let

ℓt(y)=μt+y​δt+εt(y),δt≥0,δt=0​(t∉C).\ell_{t}^{(y)}=\mu_{t}+y\delta_{t}+\varepsilon_{t}^{(y)},\qquad\delta_{t}\geq 0,\quad\delta_{t}=0\ (t\notin C). (A.18)

Within each class the noises are independent and centered, have equal variances across classes, Var⁡(εt(0))=Var⁡(εt(1))=σt2\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_{t}^{(0)})=\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_{t}^{(1)})=\sigma_{t}^{2}, and satisfy |εt(y)|≤at|\varepsilon_{t}^{(y)}|\leq a_{t}. Assume separated support,

mint∈C⁡(μt−at)>maxt∉C⁡(μt+at),\min_{t\in C}(\mu_{t}-a_{t})>\max_{t\notin C}(\mu_{t}+a_{t}), (A.19)

with the condition vacuous when CC is the whole span. Set DC=∑t∈Cδt>0D_{C}=\sum_{t\in C}\delta_{t}>0, VC=∑t∈Cσt2>0V_{C}=\sum_{t\in C}\sigma_{t}^{2}>0, and VB=∑t∉Cσt2V_{B}=\sum_{t\notin C}\sigma_{t}^{2}. For standardized pairwise separation

d⁡(S)=𝔼​SW−𝔼​SRVar⁡(SW)+Var⁡(SR),d(S)=\frac{\mathbb{E}S_{W}-\mathbb{E}S_{R}}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(S_{W})+\operatorname{Var}(S_{R})}},

the exact separation formulas are

d⁡(Tk)=DC2​VC,d⁡(ℓ¯)=DC2​(VC+VB).d(T_{k})=\frac{D_{C}}{\sqrt{2V_{C}}},\qquad d(\bar{\ell})=\frac{D_{C}}{\sqrt{2(V_{C}+V_{B})}}. (A.20)
Corollary A.2 (Separation gain comes from removing background variance).

Under (A.18)–(A.19), the ratio of tail to mean separation is

d⁡(Tk)d⁡(ℓ¯)=1+VBVC.\frac{d(T_{k})}{d(\bar{\ell})}=\sqrt{1+\frac{V_{B}}{V_{C}}}. (A.21)

With equal per-token noise variances, the ratio is L/k\sqrt{L/k}. If the background is deterministic and common to both classes, the mean and tail scores are positive affine transforms and give identical rankings.

Sparse-signal separation and Corollary A.2.

Condition (A.19) and nonnegative shifts imply that every critical position exceeds every background position almost surely in both classes. Thus the top-kk set is exactly CC before and after the class shift, and

Tk​(ℓ(y))=1k​∑t∈Cμt+y​DCk+1k​∑t∈Cεt(y).T_{k}(\bm{\ell}^{(y)})=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{t\in C}\mu_{t}+y\frac{D_{C}}{k}+\frac{1}{k}\sum_{t\in C}\varepsilon_{t}^{(y)}.

Independence and centering give class mean difference DC/kD_{C}/k and within-class variance VC/k2V_{C}/k^{2}. For the full mean the corresponding quantities are DC/LD_{C}/L and (VC+VB)/L2(V_{C}+V_{B})/L^{2}. Substitution into the definition of dd proves (A.20). With common positive variance σ2\sigma^{2}, VC=k​σ2V_{C}=k\sigma^{2} and VB=(L−k)​σ2V_{B}=(L-k)\sigma^{2}, giving ratio L/k\sqrt{L/k}.

If VB=0V_{B}=0, each background noise has zero variance and mean zero, hence is zero almost surely. Consequently

ℓ¯=kL​Tk​(ℓ)+1L​∑t∉Cμt\bar{\ell}=\frac{k}{L}T_{k}(\bm{\ell})+\frac{1}{L}\sum_{t\notin C}\mu_{t}

in both classes. The positive affine map preserves all comparisons and threshold acceptance sets, establishing the stronger equal-ranking claim. If VC=0V_{C}=0 and DC>0D_{C}>0, tail scores are deterministic and perfectly separated; the finite-SNR display omits this case only to avoid division by zero. ∎

Localized failures.

If only m≤km\leq k critical positions have a common shift Δ\Delta, then DC=m​ΔD_{C}=m\Delta, the tail’s class mean gap is m​Δ/km\Delta/k, and the whole-answer mean gap is m​Δ/Lm\Delta/L. These are exact within the model. Calling a position “critical” does not assert that a language model’s mathematical correctness follows an observed independent AND gate; that causal interpretation would require additional measurements.

What selection stability supplies.

The top-kk variance is exactly a sum of variances divided by k2k^{2} because the support separation fixes its membership. When harmless lexical spikes can enter or leave the selected set, the functional is nonlinear and that formula need not hold. Its deterministic sensitivity still holds: perturbing at most mm coordinates upward by at most uu changes TkT_{k} by at most min⁡(m/k,1)​u\min(m/k,1)u. To prove this, use ∑t∈Iwt≤min⁡(m/k,1)\sum_{t\in I}w_{t}\leq\min(m/k,1) for every feasible dual weight vector. This limits spike influence relative to a maximum without implying a distribution-free variance decay rate.

Corollary A.3 (An explicit wrong-budget operating point).

Under (A.18)–(A.19), use J=CJ=C, nJ=kn_{J}=k for the tail, or J={1,…,L}J=\{1,\ldots,L\}, nJ=Ln_{J}=L for the mean. Let mR,J=nJ−1​∑t∈Jμtm_{R,J}=n_{J}^{-1}\sum_{t\in J}\mu_{t}, mW,J=mR,J+DC/nJm_{W,J}=m_{R,J}+D_{C}/n_{J}, and AJ=∑t∈Jat2>0A_{J}=\sum_{t\in J}a_{t}^{2}>0. Let πR\pi_{R} and πW\pi_{W} be the unfiltered marginal probabilities of right and wrong submissions. For 0<α0<πW0<\alpha_{0}<\pi_{W}, define

τJ=mW,J−2​AJ​log⁡(πW/α0)nJ.\tau_{J}=m_{W,J}-\frac{\sqrt{2A_{J}\log(\pi_{W}/\alpha_{0})}}{n_{J}}. (A.22)

Accepting valid submissions with score below τJ\tau_{J} gives W⁡(τJ)≤α0W(\tau_{J})\leq\alpha_{0} and

R⁡(τJ)≥πR​[1−exp⁡{−12​(DCAJ−2​log⁡(πW/α0))+2}].R(\tau_{J})\geq\pi_{R}\left[1-\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{D_{C}}{\sqrt{A_{J}}}-\sqrt{2\log(\pi_{W}/\alpha_{0})}\right)_{+}^{2}\right\}\right]. (A.23)
Proof.

For independent, centered variables εt∈[−at,at]\varepsilon_{t}\in[-a_{t},a_{t}], Hoeffding’s inequality gives, for u>0u>0,

Pr(∑t∈Jεt≤−u)≤e−u2/(2AJ),Pr(∑t∈Jεt≥u)≤e−u2/(2AJ).\Pr\left(\sum_{t\in J}\varepsilon_{t}\leq-u\right)\leq e^{-u^{2}/(2A_{J})},\qquad\Pr\left(\sum_{t\in J}\varepsilon_{t}\geq u\right)\leq e^{-u^{2}/(2A_{J})}. (A.24)

For completeness, convexity of the exponential bounds its value at x∈[−at,at]x\in[-a_{t},a_{t}] by the chord joining its endpoint values. Taking expectations and using 𝔼​x=0\mathbb{E}x=0 gives 𝔼​es​x≤cosh⁡(s​at)≤es2​at2/2\mathbb{E}e^{sx}\leq\cosh(sa_{t})\leq e^{s^{2}a_{t}^{2}/2}. The second inequality follows by integrating tanh⁡u≤u\tanh u\leq u for u≥0u\geq 0 and using symmetry for u<0u<0. Multiplying these bounds and minimizing exp⁡(−s​u+s2​AJ/2)\exp(-su+s^{2}A_{J}/2) over s>0s>0 gives the two inequalities.

For wrong draws, nJ​(SW−mW,J)=∑t∈Jεt(1)n_{J}(S_{W}-m_{W,J})=\sum_{t\in J}\varepsilon_{t}^{(1)}. Substitution of u=2​AJ​log⁡(πW/α0)u=\sqrt{2A_{J}\log(\pi_{W}/\alpha_{0})} into (A.24) yields

W⁡(τJ)=πW​Pr⁡(SW<τJ∣W)≤α0.W(\tau_{J})=\pi_{W}\Pr(S_{W}<\tau_{J}\mid W)\leq\alpha_{0}.

For right draws,

nJ​(τJ−mR,J)=DC−2​AJ​log⁡(πW/α0).n_{J}(\tau_{J}-m_{R,J})=D_{C}-\sqrt{2A_{J}\log(\pi_{W}/\alpha_{0})}.

If this number is positive, the upper-tail Hoeffding inequality bounds the probability that a right score is at least τJ\tau_{J}. Subtracting that bound from one and multiplying by πR\pi_{R} proves (A.23). If it is nonpositive, the displayed positive-part formula reduces to the universally valid bound R≥0R\geq 0. If AJ=0A_{J}=0, the scores are deterministic and a threshold strictly between the two class means instead gives W=0W=0 and R=πRR=\pi_{R}. ∎

The bound depends on DC/AJD_{C}/\sqrt{A_{J}}, not mean dilution alone. Discarding background positions improves this sufficient guarantee by removing nuisance concentration terms while preserving the total class signal. This population threshold uses model parameters; deployment estimates its threshold by calibration. The next result connects these distinct constructions.

Corollary A.4 (Finite-calibration slack).

Let an i.i.d. calibration sample have size nn, and let the CRC rule choose the largest threshold satisfying (1+∑i=1n𝟏​{Yi=W,Si<τ})/(n+1)≤α(1+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\{Y_{i}=W,S_{i}<\tau\})/(n+1)\leq\alpha, with the usual strict-tie convention. Fix a calibration slack satisfying

1−αn<η<α,\frac{1-\alpha}{n}<\eta<\alpha,

and a data-independent threshold τ0\tau_{0} with population W⁡(τ0)≤α−ηW(\tau_{0})\leq\alpha-\eta. Then

Pr⁡(τ^CRC≥τ0)≥1−exp⁡[−2​n​(η−1−αn)2].\Pr(\widehat{\tau}_{\rm CRC}\geq\tau_{0})\geq 1-\exp\left[-2n\left(\eta-\frac{1-\alpha}{n}\right)^{2}\right]. (A.25)

On this event R⁡(τ^CRC)≥R⁡(τ0)R(\widehat{\tau}_{\rm CRC})\geq R(\tau_{0}). In particular, choosing τ0\tau_{0} from Corollary A.3 with α0=α−η<πW\alpha_{0}=\alpha-\eta<\pi_{W} transfers its correct-submission lower bound to the CRC policy on the displayed high-probability event.

Proof.

The calibration wrong-submission indicators at τ0\tau_{0} are i.i.d. Bernoulli with mean at most α−η\alpha-\eta. The threshold is feasible whenever their average is at most α−(1−α)/n\alpha-(1-\alpha)/n. Hoeffding’s inequality therefore bounds the probability of infeasibility by the exponential in (A.25). Whenever τ0\tau_{0} is feasible, the maximal feasible CRC threshold is at least τ0\tau_{0}, including the strict-tie implementation. Acceptance is monotone in the threshold, so its correct-submission probability is at least that at τ0\tau_{0}. The efficiency bound assumes an explicit population margin and i.i.d. calibration; the marginal CRC guarantee is separate. ∎

An optional exact ROC interpretation.

In the separate score-level model SR∼N⁡(μR,σ2)S_{R}\sim N(\mu_{R},\sigma^{2}) and SW∼N⁡(μW,σ2)S_{W}\sim N(\mu_{W},\sigma^{2}), put d0=(μW−μR)/σd_{0}=(\mu_{W}-\mu_{R})/\sigma. At 0<α<πW0<\alpha<\pi_{W}, the threshold τ=μW+σ​Φ−1​(α/πW)\tau=\mu_{W}+\sigma\Phi^{-1}(\alpha/\pi_{W}) has

W=α,R=πR​Φ​(Φ−1​(α/πW)+d0),AUC=Φ⁡(d0/2).W=\alpha,\qquad R=\pi_{R}\Phi\left(\Phi^{-1}(\alpha/\pi_{W})+d_{0}\right),\qquad\operatorname{AUC}=\Phi(d_{0}/\sqrt{2}).

These identities follow from the two normal CDFs and the normal law of SW−SRS_{W}-S_{R}. They show how stronger standardized separation can retain more correct submissions at a fixed wrong budget. This Gaussian score model differs from the bounded, separated-support token model: nondegenerate Gaussian token noise is unbounded and cannot satisfy almost-sure support separation.

A maximum can be dominated by nuisance extremes.

This is a separate illustrative model, not an assumption of the preceding sparse-signal analysis. Suppose all class-dependent critical scores are bounded above by KK, and there are mm independent class-independent nuisance scores with common CDF FF, where F⁡(K)<1F(K)<1. Couple the maximum score in each class to its nuisance-only maximum. They differ only if every nuisance score is at most KK, an event of probability F​(K)mF(K)^{m}. The independent nuisance-only maxima have tie-corrected AUROC 1/21/2 by symmetry. A union bound over the two class draws yields

|AUC⁡(max)−12|≤2​F​(K)m.\left|\operatorname{AUC}(\max)-\tfrac{1}{2}\right|\leq 2F(K)^{m}.

The conclusion follows because the pairwise AUROC contribution lies in [0,1][0,1] and is unchanged when both coupled scores agree. This provides one precise way that a maximum can lose signal. It does not establish that every upper-tail average avoids nuisance contamination. Under a specific tail model, a growing expected maximum alone implies neither growing variance nor declining AUROC.

A.6.4 Decoder-aware martingales and stopping

Token log probabilities are available with many generation APIs, whereas full-vocabulary entropy requires access to the model distribution at each prefix. The additional access is valuable only if it changes the information used to rank answers. To examine that question, we separate the uncertainty of the model distribution from the random surprise of the token actually sampled, accounting for the decoder transformation used by the experiments. This distinction is essential because top-pp/top-kk sampling generally changes the distribution from which a token is drawn.

Proposition A.2 (Decoder-aware surprise and a sharp tail comparison).

At generation history ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1}, let ptp_{t} be the scored token distribution and qtq_{t} the actual sampling distribution on a finite vocabulary, with qt≪ptq_{t}\ll p_{t} and finite surprise second moment. For Yt∼qtY_{t}\sim q_{t} conditionally,

ℓt\displaystyle\ell_{t} =−log⁡pt​(Yt)=H⁡(pt)+bt+ξt,\displaystyle=-\log p_{t}(Y_{t})=H(p_{t})+b_{t}+\xi_{t},
ct\displaystyle c_{t} =H(qt)+DKL(qt∥pt),bt=ct−H(pt),\displaystyle=H(q_{t})+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_{t}\|p_{t}),\qquad b_{t}=c_{t}-H(p_{t}),
𝔼⁡[ξt∣ℱt−1]\displaystyle\E[\xi_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}] =0,𝔼⁡[ξt2∣ℱt−1]=vt:=Varqt⁡[−log⁡pt​(Yt)].\displaystyle=0,\qquad\E[\xi_{t}^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]=v_{t}:=\operatorname{Var}_{q_{t}}[-\log p_{t}(Y_{t})]. (A.26)

For a deterministic horizon NN, the mean residual N−1​∑t=1NξtN^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\xi_{t} has second moment N−2​∑t=1N𝔼⁡vtN^{-2}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\E v_{t}. When qt=ptq_{t}=p_{t}, bt=0b_{t}=0 and vtv_{t} is token varentropy. For every realized scored span, write rt=ℓt−H⁡(pt)r_{t}=\ell_{t}-H(p_{t}) and r¯=L−1​∑trt\bar{r}=L^{-1}\sum_{t}r_{t}. Then

|Tk​(ℓ)−Tk​(𝐇)−r¯|≤1k−1L​‖𝐫−r¯​𝟏‖2,\left|T_{k}(\bm{\ell})-T_{k}(\mathbf{H})-\bar{r}\right|\leq\sqrt{\frac{1}{k}-\frac{1}{L}}\,\|\mathbf{r}-\bar{r}\mathbf{1}\|_{2}, (A.27)

with a sharp constant, including for random-length or validity-selected spans.

Proof. The decomposition and isometry are proved below; Appendix A.6.5 proves the pathwise bound.

The decomposition identifies three contributions to sampled-token surprise: full-distribution entropy H⁡(pt)H(p_{t}), decoder drift btb_{t}, and centered random surprise ξt\xi_{t}. At temperature one, truncation to a retained set with probability mass ZtZ_{t} gives ct=H⁡(qt)−log⁡Ztc_{t}=H(q_{t})-\log Z_{t}. Full-vocabulary entropy removes sampled-token fluctuation but also changes the decoder-dependent center, making its effect on answer ranking an empirical question.

A simple example distinguishes entropy from sampling noise. A uniform model distribution on KK tokens has entropy log⁡K\log K, yet every token has the same surprise and varentropy is zero [18]. High entropy alone therefore does not predict an entropy upgrade. In a fixed-context resampling model, convexity gives 𝔼⁡Tk​(ℓ)−Tk​(𝐜)≥0\E T_{k}(\bm{\ell})-T_{k}(\mathbf{c})\geq 0, with an upper bound in terms of vtv_{t}; matched sampling specializes the center to entropy. Lemma A.3 translates score perturbations into ranking changes through right–wrong pair margins.

For a deterministic horizon NN, the precise isometry is

𝔼​(1N​∑t=1Nξt)2=1N2​∑t=1N𝔼​vt.\mathbb{E}\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\xi_{t}\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}v_{t}. (A.28)
Decomposition and isometry in Proposition A.2.

Conditional on ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1}, both distributions are fixed and YtY_{t} is distributed according to qtq_{t}. Therefore

𝔼⁡[ℓt∣ℱt−1]=∑vqt​(v)​[−log⁡pt​(v)]=ct.\mathbb{E}[\ell_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]=\sum_{v}q_{t}(v)[-\log p_{t}(v)]=c_{t}.

Centering proves both conditional-moment statements. Adding and subtracting H⁡(pt)H(p_{t}) gives (A.26). The cross-entropy identity follows from −log⁡pt​(v)=−log⁡qt​(v)+log⁡(qt​(v)/pt​(v))-\log p_{t}(v)=-\log q_{t}(v)+\log(q_{t}(v)/p_{t}(v)) on the support of qtq_{t}.

For s<ts<t, ξs\xi_{s} is ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1}-measurable, so integrability and the tower property imply

𝔼⁡[ξs​ξt]=𝔼⁡[ξs​𝔼​(ξt∣ℱt−1)]=0.\mathbb{E}[\xi_{s}\xi_{t}]=\mathbb{E}[\xi_{s}\mathbb{E}(\xi_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1})]=0.

Thus expanding the square of the deterministic-horizon sum eliminates all cross terms, and

𝔼​(∑t=1Nξt)2=∑t=1N𝔼​ξt2=∑t=1N𝔼​vt.\mathbb{E}\left(\sum_{t=1}^{N}\xi_{t}\right)^{2}=\sum_{t=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}\xi_{t}^{2}=\sum_{t=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}v_{t}.

Division by N2N^{2} proves (A.28). The sum has mean zero, so this second moment is its variance. The same identities hold conditionally on the initial sigma-field ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0} after replacing each outer expectation by its conditional version. Conditioning on the entire random future history need not preserve orthogonality.

When qt=ptq_{t}=p_{t}, ct=H⁡(pt)c_{t}=H(p_{t}) and its conditional variance is V⁡(pt)=∑vpt​(v)​[−log⁡pt​(v)−H⁡(pt)]2V(p_{t})=\sum_{v}p_{t}(v)[-\log p_{t}(v)-H(p_{t})]^{2}. For truncation, on the retained support −log⁡pt​(v)=−log⁡qt​(v)−log⁡Zt-\log p_{t}(v)=-\log q_{t}(v)-\log Z_{t}. Taking its qtq_{t}-mean proves ct=H⁡(qt)−log⁡Ztc_{t}=H(q_{t})-\log Z_{t}; subtracting its mean cancels the constant −log⁡Zt-\log Z_{t}, proving vt=V⁡(qt)v_{t}=V(q_{t}). ∎

For a retained set consisting of the most probable tokens, every retained surprise is no greater than every omitted surprise. If 0<Zt<10<Z_{t}<1 and ctoutc_{t}^{\rm out} is the mean surprise conditional on omission,

bt=ct−H⁡(pt)=(1−Zt)​(ct−ctout)≤0.b_{t}=c_{t}-H(p_{t})=(1-Z_{t})(c_{t}-c_{t}^{\rm out})\leq 0.

Its magnitude can vary with context. A small measured discrepancy between receipt log probabilities and recomputed raw log probabilities does not set Zt=1Z_{t}=1 or remove this drift: it compares scoring values, not the two sampling laws. If a receipt log probability has an additional numerical or backend residual ete_{t} relative to −log⁡pt​(Yt)-\log p_{t}(Y_{t}), the exact pathwise residual becomes rt=bt+ξt+etr_{t}=b_{t}+\xi_{t}+e_{t}.

Lemma A.2 (Predictable weighting and bounded stopping).

If ata_{t} is ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1}-measurable and the terms are square integrable, the weighted sum has zero mean and satisfies the isometry

𝔼​∑t=1Nat​ξt=0,𝔼​(∑t=1Nat​ξt)2=𝔼​∑t=1Nat2​vt.\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{N}a_{t}\xi_{t}=0,\qquad\mathbb{E}\left(\sum_{t=1}^{N}a_{t}\xi_{t}\right)^{2}=\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{N}a_{t}^{2}v_{t}.

In particular, for a stopping time τ≤N\tau\leq N,

𝔼​∑t=1τξt=0,𝔼​(∑t=1τξt)2=𝔼​∑t=1τvt.\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{\tau}\xi_{t}=0,\qquad\mathbb{E}\left(\sum_{t=1}^{\tau}\xi_{t}\right)^{2}=\mathbb{E}\sum_{t=1}^{\tau}v_{t}.
Proof.

The weighted increments have conditional mean zero and conditional second moment at2​vta_{t}^{2}v_{t}. The preceding orthogonality proof applies to them unchanged. For bounded stopping, use at=𝟏{τ≥t}a_{t}=\mathbf{1}\{\tau\geq t\}. This is predictable because {τ≥t}\{\tau\geq t\} is the complement of {τ≤t−1}∈ℱt−1\{\tau\leq t-1\}\in\mathcal{F}_{t-1}. ∎

If τ\tau is the first EOS time, these statements include its sampled EOS token. The indicator for retaining a token strictly before EOS is 𝟏{t<τ}\mathbf{1}\{t<\tau\}, which depends on the current token and need not be predictable. Deleting EOS therefore changes the compensator. One can center a masked contribution directly, for example gt(Yt)=𝟏{Yt≠EOS}[−logpt(Yt)]g_{t}(Y_{t})=\mathbf{1}\{Y_{t}\neq\mathrm{EOS}\}[-\log p_{t}(Y_{t})], by ∑vqt​(v)​gt​(v)\sum_{v}q_{t}(v)g_{t}(v), but that center is not Shannon entropy. Selecting only eventually valid trajectories is another conditioning operation depending on future tokens. Neither operation preserves the unconditioned martingale statements automatically.

Random normalization can introduce bias.

An example uses genuine self-information. Draw two independent tokens from p=(2/3,1/3)p=(2/3,1/3), and let a=(log⁡2)/3a=(\log 2)/3. Their centered surprises independently equal −a-a with probability 2/32/3 and 2​a2a with probability 1/31/3. Stop at τ=1\tau=1 if the first centered surprise is 2​a2a, and at τ=2\tau=2 otherwise. This is a bounded stopping time, and the unnormalized stopped sum has mean zero. Normalizing by the stopping time instead gives a nonzero expectation:

𝔼⁡[1τ​∑t=1τξt]=a3≠0.\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{\tau}\sum_{t=1}^{\tau}\xi_{t}\right]=\frac{a}{3}\neq 0.

Indeed, the normalized sum takes values 2​a,a/2,−a2a,a/2,-a with probabilities 1/3,2/9,4/91/3,2/9,4/9. Its second moment is 11​a2/611a^{2}/6, whereas naively placing the random denominator in the deterministic-horizon formula would give

𝔼⁡[1τ2​∑t=1τvt]=𝔼⁡[2​a2τ]=4​a23.\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{\tau^{2}}\sum_{t=1}^{\tau}v_{t}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{2a^{2}}{\tau}\right]=\frac{4a^{2}}{3}.

The discrepancy is not a minor asymptotic technicality. It excludes an exact unbiasedness or variance claim for the random-length answer mean without additional conditions.

A.6.5 A pathwise bound that survives span selection

The pathwise bound is tailored to the implemented answer score. A fixed horizon gives a martingale second-moment identity, but the scored span ends at a random time, excludes EOS, and is evaluated among valid outputs. Equation (A.27) continues to hold for each such realized span. It shows that the discrepancy between tail surprise and tail entropy depends on the mean residual and its variation across positions: uniform shifts and localized spikes affect the tail differently.

Pathwise bound in Proposition A.2.

Let 𝒲k={w:0≤wt≤1/k,∑twt=1}\mathcal{W}_{k}=\{w:0\leq w_{t}\leq 1/k,\sum_{t}w_{t}=1\}, u=L−1​𝟏u=L^{-1}\mathbf{1}, and z∘=z−z¯​𝟏z^{\circ}=z-\bar{z}\mathbf{1}. For any w∈𝒲kw\in\mathcal{W}_{k}, its coordinate bounds and unit sum imply

‖w−u‖22=∑twt2−1L≤1k​∑twt−1L=1k−1L.\|w-u\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{t}w_{t}^{2}-\frac{1}{L}\leq\frac{1}{k}\sum_{t}w_{t}-\frac{1}{L}=\frac{1}{k}-\frac{1}{L}.

If w+w_{+} maximizes Tk​(x+z)T_{k}(x+z), then Tk​(x+z)−Tk​(x)≤w+⊤​zT_{k}(x+z)-T_{k}(x)\leq w_{+}^{\top}z. If w0w_{0} maximizes Tk​(x)T_{k}(x), the analogous lower bound is Tk​(x+z)−Tk​(x)≥w0⊤​zT_{k}(x+z)-T_{k}(x)\geq w_{0}^{\top}z. Since

w⊤​z=z¯+(w−u)⊤​z∘,w^{\top}z=\bar{z}+(w-u)^{\top}z^{\circ},

Cauchy–Schwarz bounds deviations from z¯\bar{z} by 1/k−1/L​‖z∘‖2\sqrt{1/k-1/L}\|z^{\circ}\|_{2}. Set x=𝐇x=\mathbf{H}, z=ℓ−𝐇z=\bm{\ell}-\mathbf{H} to obtain (A.27).

For sharpness when k<Lk<L, choose a fixed kk-subset JJ, w=𝟏J/kw=\mathbf{1}_{J}/k, x=0x=0, and z=w−uz=w-u. Then z¯=0\bar{z}=0, its top-kk subset is JJ, and

Tk​(z)=w⊤​(w−u)=1k−1L,‖z‖2=1k−1L.T_{k}(z)=w^{\top}(w-u)=\frac{1}{k}-\frac{1}{L},\qquad\|z\|_{2}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{k}-\frac{1}{L}}.

Equality holds. When k=Lk=L, TkT_{k} is the mean and the bound is the identity with zero remainder. No part of the proof used a distribution for x,z,Lx,z,L, so it remains true after any span or validity selection. ∎

A weaker but sometimes convenient consequence of the dual representation is

|Tk​(x+z)−Tk​(x)|≤min⁡{‖z‖∞,‖z‖1/k,‖z‖2/k}.|T_{k}(x+z)-T_{k}(x)|\leq\min\{\|z\|_{\infty},\ \|z\|_{1}/k,\ \|z\|_{2}/\sqrt{k}\}.

The centered bound distinguishes an overall score displacement from heterogeneous fluctuations that can alter which tokens enter the tail.

A.6.6 Fixed-context convexity, equality, and autoregressive limits

In a separate fixed-context perturbation model, hold p1:L,q1:Lp_{1:L},q_{1:L} fixed exogenously and draw independent tokens from the qtq_{t}. Then

0≤𝔼​Tk​(ℓ)−Tk​(𝐜)≤(1k−1L)​(1−1L)​∑t=1Lvt.0\leq\mathbb{E}T_{k}(\bm{\ell})-T_{k}(\mathbf{c})\leq\sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{k}-\frac{1}{L}\right)\left(1-\frac{1}{L}\right)\sum_{t=1}^{L}v_{t}}. (A.29)

Equality on the left holds exactly when some fixed kk-element subset is a maximizing subset almost surely. Zero varentropy is sufficient in the matched-law case, but is not necessary.

Fixed-context extension of Proposition A.2.

Hold the distributions fixed exogenously. The deterministic mean vector is 𝐜\mathbf{c} and ℓ=𝐜+𝝃\bm{\ell}=\mathbf{c}+\bm{\xi}, with 𝔼​𝝃=0\mathbb{E}\bm{\xi}=0. Equation (11) expresses TkT_{k} as a maximum of linear functions, so it is convex. Jensen’s inequality gives 𝔼​Tk​(ℓ)≥Tk​(𝐜)\mathbb{E}T_{k}(\bm{\ell})\geq T_{k}(\mathbf{c}). The pathwise upper bound gives

Tk​(𝐜+𝝃)−Tk​(𝐜)≤ξ¯+1/k−1/L​‖𝝃−ξ¯​𝟏‖2.T_{k}(\mathbf{c}+\bm{\xi})-T_{k}(\mathbf{c})\leq\bar{\xi}+\sqrt{1/k-1/L}\|\bm{\xi}-\bar{\xi}\mathbf{1}\|_{2}.

Its expectation is at most

1/k−1/L​𝔼​‖𝝃−ξ¯​𝟏‖22.\sqrt{1/k-1/L}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\|\bm{\xi}-\bar{\xi}\mathbf{1}\|_{2}^{2}}.

Independence and centering imply 𝔼​ξ¯2=L−2​∑tvt\mathbb{E}\bar{\xi}^{2}=L^{-2}\sum_{t}v_{t}. Hence

𝔼​‖𝝃−ξ¯​𝟏‖22=∑tvt−L​𝔼​ξ¯2=(1−1/L)​∑tvt,\mathbb{E}\|\bm{\xi}-\bar{\xi}\mathbf{1}\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{t}v_{t}-L\mathbb{E}\bar{\xi}^{2}=(1-1/L)\sum_{t}v_{t},

proving (A.29). Jensen itself does not require independence. For dependent perturbations with covariance matrix Σ\Sigma, the same proof replaces the final factor by tr⁡Σ−L−1​𝟏⊤​Σ​𝟏\operatorname{tr}\Sigma-L^{-1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}\Sigma\mathbf{1}.

For equality, choose a deterministic kk-subset JJ maximizing the mean vector 𝐜\mathbf{c}. Then

Tk​(ℓ)−1k​∑t∈Jℓt≥0almost surely,T_{k}(\bm{\ell})-\frac{1}{k}\sum_{t\in J}\ell_{t}\geq 0\quad\text{almost surely},

and its expectation equals 𝔼​Tk​(ℓ)−Tk​(𝐜)\mathbb{E}T_{k}(\bm{\ell})-T_{k}(\mathbf{c}). That expectation is zero exactly when the nonnegative random variable is zero almost surely, i.e. when JJ is maximizing almost surely. Conversely, if a fixed JJ is maximizing almost surely, its expected value is at least that of every other subset, so it also maximizes the mean vector and the gap is zero. This proves the stated necessary and sufficient condition, including ties and k=Lk=L. ∎

Positive varentropy with zero Jensen gap.

For L=2,k=1L=2,k=1, take independent matched-law tokens from p1=(2/3,1/3)p_{1}=(2/3,1/3) and p2=(0.3,0.3,0.2,0.2)p_{2}=(0.3,0.3,0.2,0.2). Both distributions have positive varentropy. Every first-coordinate surprise is at most log⁡3\log 3, while every second-coordinate surprise is at least log⁡(10/3)>log⁡3\log(10/3)>\log 3. The second coordinate is therefore always the maximum, and

𝔼​max⁡(ℓ1,ℓ2)=H⁡(p2)=max⁡(H⁡(p1),H⁡(p2)).\mathbb{E}\max(\ell_{1},\ell_{2})=H(p_{2})=\max(H(p_{1}),H(p_{2})).

Repeating the low-support distribution at nine positions and using the high-support distribution at one gives the same counterexample for the literal L=10,k=1L=10,k=1 tail10 score. Zero varentropy is therefore not necessary, even if every coordinate has positive varentropy. For a finite distribution pp, V⁡(p)=0V(p)=0 itself is equivalent to uniformity on its positive-probability support: zero variance forces −log⁡p⁡(Y)-\log p(Y) to be constant, so all positive probabilities coincide; the converse is immediate.

The fixed-context bias need not disappear with length.

For example, let all coordinates be independent draws from p=(0.9,0.1)p=(0.9,0.1) and let k=⌈0.1​L⌉k=\lceil 0.1L\rceil. The two surprise values are a=−log⁡0.9a=-\log 0.9 and b=−log⁡0.1b=-\log 0.1. If NLN_{L} is the number of rare draws, then

Tk​(ℓ)=a+(b−a)​min⁡(NL/k,1).T_{k}(\bm{\ell})=a+(b-a)\min(N_{L}/k,1).

The law of large numbers gives NL/L→0.1N_{L}/L\to 0.1 and k/L→0.1k/L\to 0.1, so Tk​(ℓ)→bT_{k}(\bm{\ell})\to b almost surely. Bounded convergence then transfers this almost-sure limit to the expected score:

𝔼​Tk​(ℓ)−Tk​(𝐇)⟶b−H⁡(p)>0.\mathbb{E}T_{k}(\bm{\ell})-T_{k}(\mathbf{H})\longrightarrow b-H(p)>0.

Thus a finite-sample upper-tail selection bias can remain of constant order at a fixed tail fraction, even with independent coordinates. The bound in (A.29) is consistent: for equal vt=vv_{t}=v and fixed k/Lk/L, it is of order v\sqrt{v}, not L−1/2L^{-1/2}. At fixed LL, the bound vanishes with the coordinate varentropies.

Autoregression can reverse the Jensen comparison.

Consider a deterministic horizon L=10L=10, k=1k=1, with matched sampling law qt=ptq_{t}=p_{t}. At the first step, p1=(0.9,0.1)p_{1}=(0.9,0.1). If the common token is drawn, let step two be deterministic. If the rare token is drawn, let step two be uniform on ten tokens. Steps three through ten are deterministic. On the common-token branch, T1​(ℓ)=−log⁡0.9T_{1}(\bm{\ell})=-\log 0.9 while T1​(𝐇)=H⁡(p1)T_{1}(\mathbf{H})=H(p_{1}). On the rare-token branch, both equal log⁡10\log 10. Consequently

𝔼​T1​(ℓ)−𝔼​T1​(𝐇)=0.9​[−log⁡0.9−H⁡(p1)]<0.\mathbb{E}T_{1}(\bm{\ell})-\mathbb{E}T_{1}(\mathbf{H})=0.9[-\log 0.9-H(p_{1})]<0.

Every per-step conditional-mean identity is valid, but the sequence of later distributions reveals the first draw. Conditioning on that sequence is therefore not the independent resampling experiment used in (A.29). This also shows why Tk​(𝐇)T_{k}(\mathbf{H}) should not be described as the exact Rao–Blackwell conditional expectation of the entire sampled tail score.

A.6.7 From score discrepancies to ranking discrepancies

Lemma A.3 (A score-margin condition for AUROC proximity).

Let two scores S,TS,T be coupled on the same trajectory. On independent right and wrong draws write ey=Sy−Tye_{y}=S_{y}-T_{y}. Then

|AUC⁡(S)−AUC⁡(T)|≤Pr⁡(|TW−TR|≤|eW|+|eR|).|\operatorname{AUC}(S)-\operatorname{AUC}(T)|\leq\Pr\bigl(|T_{W}-T_{R}|\leq|e_{W}|+|e_{R}|\bigr). (A.30)

In particular, for any ϵR,ϵW≥0\epsilon_{R},\epsilon_{W}\geq 0, the right side is at most

Pr⁡(|TW−TR|≤ϵR+ϵW)+Pr⁡(|eR|>ϵR)+Pr⁡(|eW|>ϵW).\Pr\bigl(|T_{W}-T_{R}|\leq\epsilon_{R}+\epsilon_{W}\bigr)+\Pr(|e_{R}|>\epsilon_{R})+\Pr(|e_{W}|>\epsilon_{W}).
Proof.

Outside the event on the right of (A.30), the perturbation eW−eRe_{W}-e_{R} is strictly smaller in absolute value than TW−TRT_{W}-T_{R}, so it cannot change its sign or create a tie. Thus the two pairwise ψ\psi contributions agree there. On the event they can differ by at most one. Taking expectations proves the first bound; splitting according to the two error events proves the second. ∎

The lemma supplies a sufficient route from a small pathwise discrepancy to similar AUROC: pairwise entropy-score margins must also be large relative to that discrepancy. The converse fails. Large changes that preserve rankings can leave AUROC unchanged, and equal aggregate AUROCs can arise from different pairs changing in opposite directions. Hence neither an equal AUROC nor a confidence interval crossing zero supports an estimate of low varentropy. The empirical comparison and the conditional mathematical mechanisms must remain separate claims.

B.2 Exact decoding and scoring conventions

For Qwen3.5-4B, OPEN is (248068,198)(248068,198), CLOSE is (248069,198)(248069,198), and chat EOS is 248046. For Qwen3-8B they are (151667,198)(151667,198), (151668,198)(151668,198), and 151645. OPEN occurs once in the assistant prefix. The nominal cap includes this prefill and any two-token external CLOSE. At 4K, the two sampled segment caps are 2,046 and 2,046; at 8K they are 4,094 and 4,094. A naturally generated CLOSE does not trigger another injected delimiter. An early terminal ends the request, and the second call continues the existing prefix if needed. There are no custom stop strings. Sampling seeds are deterministic per family, model/budget, and segment, with common seeds across compared arms within the same decoder. Native and ExtBF use different segment streams and are paired by family, not by identical sampled trajectories.

The verifier first checks whether a completed, extractable mathematical answer was submitted. Normal chat EOS and mutually equivalent extracted boxes are required for a tolerant valid submission. Truncation, conflicting boxes, or other invalid structure yields UU. The tolerant correctness check uses math-verify 0.9.0. Strict-format correctness is a separate diagnostic, which can mark repeated equivalent boxes invalid even when their value is correct. S3A identifies explicit abstention only after the first CLOSE and normal EOS, when all valid boxed contents match ABSTAIN after whitespace and text wrapper normalization, without case sensitivity. Such cases are UabstainU_{\mathrm{abstain}} and, like truncation, receive zero reward.

The scored answer span consists only of sampled tokens after the first CLOSE and before EOS. Injected delimiters and injected newline tokens, and EOS itself, are excluded. For length LL, let k=⌈L/10⌉k=\lceil L/10\rceil; tail10_nll is the mean of the largest kk sampled-token NLLs. The empirical CVaR interpretation uses effective tail fraction k/Lk/L. ans_mean_nll, ans_sum_nll, and ans_len use the same answer span. box_sum_nll includes complete generated tokens whose byte spans overlap the content of the final valid box, rather than indiscriminately including every box delimiter. Invalid submissions are always excluded from acceptance. CRC uses strict S<τS<\tau and rejects the entire group tied at the cutoff; calibration is separate for each model, seed, budget, score, and target. The allowance is ⌊(n+1)​α−1⌋\lfloor(n+1)\alpha-1\rfloor calibration wrong submissions. An all-reject fallback and the all-valid-accept case are retained explicitly.

Full-vocabulary A2 scores are computed by replaying the original token sequence, taking the previous-position hidden state and output projection, and applying FP32 softmax to BF16 model output. Tail entropy averages the largest kk entropies. The margin control averages the smallest kk top-one minus top-two probability margins, then reverses sign for the wrong-positive AUROC. Theoretical interpretation must distinguish raw-model probabilities from the top-pp/top-kk sampling distribution.

B.3 Training, masks, and baseline provenance

The mainline Dr. GRPO optimizer uses AdamW with learning rate 10−510^{-5}, β1=.9\beta_{1}=.9, β2=.95\beta_{2}=.95, ϵ=10−8\epsilon=10^{-8}, zero weight decay, and gradient-norm clipping at 1. Rank and LoRA alpha are both 32. Each of the 50 updates uses 16 prompts with eight on-policy rollouts each. The 400-family pool is traversed twice in a seed-specific deterministic order. G0’s reward is the tolerant-valid mathematical RR indicator, not a strict-format indicator. G1/S3B change the wrong-answer reward to −1/−0.25-1/-0.25; no penalty is added to invalid or truncated trajectories. The policy-gradient loss includes policy-sampled positions in both stages and excludes prompt, prefilled OPEN, and external CLOSE positions. Masked-label perturbation tests keep the input context fixed. In both supplementary-arm smoke tests, changing the masked CLOSE labels changes the loss by exactly zero; changing the actual input context does change it. Formal training restarts from the unchanged zero-update state after these disposable one-step tests.

The historical SFT diagnostic and the current SFT control are different experiments. In the earlier 16K study, M2 versus M1 was evaluated on 1,000 DAPO families with two training seeds. The strict-format improvement was 10.30 pp [8.05,12.60][8.05,12.60]; the mathematical-equivalence improvement was 1.10 pp [−.45,2.65][-.45,2.65], and their paired difference was 9.20 pp [7.25,11.20][7.25,11.20]. Its primary gate failed. The current 8B M541 control uses answer-only SFT on a 262-family rescue-inclusive pool, selecting each family’s shortest qualifying strict-correct teacher trajectory. Its own preregistration specifies batch size eight and 160 updates. The 4B E1 control is the archived answer-focused SFT policy. Neither is the earlier M2–M1 intervention.

B.4 Data selection, labels, and blinding

DAPO families use normalized text, numeric templates, and character 3–5-gram similarity at cosine threshold .90. All DAPO TEST references are bare integers. Historical Omni200 was enriched for non-bare reference answers and is only a diagnostic panel. Fresh Omni confirmation uses the pinned 4,428-row release with 4,391 families. Historical enrollment across 23 Omni panels is excluded along all three identity axes. The final eligible frame contains 1,084 verifiable remaining families. Deterministic SHA-256 ordering selects 600 without a bare/non-bare quota: CAL has 39 bare and 261 non-bare references; TEST has 37 and 263. The other 484 are reserved and untouched. This is absence of overlap with tracked study exposures, not a claim about pretraining contamination or about unverifiable excluded problems.

The OOD protocol was registered at 2026-11-21 19:28:52 UTC. CAL labels opened at 2026-11-22 01:00:58 UTC, after all study trajectories had been generated. Thresholds were locked at 01:01:48.282 UTC; TEST labels opened at 01:01:48.350 UTC. Track A transfers fixed source-DAPO cuts without a distribution-shift guarantee; Track B fits on target CAL300. Registered later at 04:05:42 UTC, the final supplement reuses released panels. Its additional controls and analyses are not fresh confirmatory endpoints.

B.5 Study sequence and prespecified outcomes

The initial 8B single-seed RL pilot’s registered DEV200 verdict was STOP_RLVR_SCALE. A separate retrospective DEV probe nominated box_sum_nll for the source-domain confirmation (2A). Its primary gates were all at BF4; BF8 and comparisons with M5 were secondary. At α=0.065\alpha=0.065, 4B pooled G0 passed against raw ExtBF base, with Δ​R=26.70\Delta R=26.70 pp (95% CI [23.10,30.40][23.10,30.40] pp) and W=5.0%W=5.0\%. Both seeds accepted every valid answer at this cutoff, so that operating point’s gain comes from solving and completion. For 8B at the same target, the comparison with raw ExtBF base gave Δ​R=3.90\Delta R=3.90 pp (95% CI [0.20,7.60][0.20,7.60] pp) and W=7.5%W=7.5\%, missing the 4 pp effect gate and the risk gate. At α=0.10\alpha=0.10, the comparison with raw G1 gave Δ​R=7.20\Delta R=7.20 pp (95% CI [3.30,11.20][3.30,11.20] pp) and W=11.5%W=11.5\%, passing the effect gate but missing the risk gate. Both 8B joint gates failed. These original endpoints use Box NLL; Tail NLL was analyzed later.

Historical Omni200 was enriched for non-bare reference answers and served as a score diagnostic. For 8B pooled G0, Box NLL AUROC was 0.544 at 4K and 0.510 at 8K. At the transferred 4K cut fitted with α=0.065\alpha=0.065, all 23 accepted wrong answers were bare-integer predictions, while 82 of 84 rejected correct answers were non-bare (400 seed–family records from two seeds). Subsequent natural-Omni TEST300 independently tested Tail NLL; it is a different panel with no answer-shape quota.

The independent Omni study passed H1a (4B raw solving and lower cost at both caps), H1b (8B raw solving at 4K), and H2a (8B Tail NLL versus Box NLL AUROC with positive 4B ordering). H2b, the joint 8B Track A net-score improvement check at both caps, failed: the Tail NLL minus Box NLL gain was 3.50 pp (95% CI [−1.00,8.33][-1.00,8.33] pp) at 4K and 5.17 pp (95% CI [0.33,10.17][0.33,10.17] pp) at 8K; the 4K interval crossed zero. H3a/H3b were reporting items for target-domain risk and LTT issuance. The later fixed-panel supplement adds Native controls, reward ablations, white-box scoring, and DAPO Tail NLL analyses.

The original 2A family bootstrap uses RNG seed 20261121; the independent Omni study and final supplement use 20261122, each with 20,000 paired resamples. White-box AUROC intervals use up to 2,000 estimable paired resamples. The Native-transfer supplement evaluates G0 seed 41 against the original Native model: all four 4B correct-submission differences have positive lower bounds (DAPO 4K/8K: 1.60/7.20 pp; Omni 4K/8K: 2.67/3.33 pp), whereas all four 8B intervals cross zero (point estimates from −0.40-0.40 to +0.60+0.60 pp). No noninferiority margin was registered. Table 6 preserves the full intervals.

B.6 LTT grids and the scope of guarantees

The two fixed cutoff grids are

𝒯tail\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{tail}} ={.50,.75,1.00,1.25,1.50,1.75,2.00,2.35,2.80,∞},\displaystyle=\{.50,.75,1.00,1.25,1.50,1.75,2.00,2.35,2.80,\infty\},
𝒯mean\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{mean}} ={.06,.10,.14,.18,.22,.27,.33,.40,.50,∞}.\displaystyle=\{.06,.10,.14,.18,.22,.27,.33,.40,.50,\infty\}.

For each fixed model, budget, score, and conditional-error target, the ten CAL binomial tests each use level .01, giving nominal δ=.10\delta=.10 across that grid. The largest passing cutoff is selected (equivalently maximum accepted coverage, with the largest cut breaking ties); if none passes, no certificate is issued. Empty acceptance sets do not certify an undefined conditional error. The target grid is {.10,.15,.20,.30}\{.10,.15,.20,.30\}; the .10 familywise guarantee does not jointly cover different targets, models, budgets, or scores.

The Omni grids were registered before its CAL release. The DAPO S1 replay uses the same recorded grids on already released CAL500/TEST500, and its provenance does not establish independence of grid construction from those calibration data. We retain its empirical counts as retrospective diagnostics. The theoretical statement requires a grid fixed independently of CAL; holding a data-chosen grid fixed during replay alone does not establish that premise. The TEST Clopper–Pearson bound is a separate description of the selected policy, not the p-value used to issue it.

Appendix C Expanded quantitative diagnostics

C.1 Raw solver contrasts and score behavior

Near-zero box NLL is not specific to KL-free RL. On DAPO 8B 4K, the median box NLL is 1.29×10−101.29\times 10^{-10} for M5, 8.92×10−88.92\times 10^{-8} for base, 1.55×10−71.55\times 10^{-7} for G1, and 5.80×10−75.80\times 10^{-7} for pooled G0. The fractions below 10−510^{-5} are 90.16%, 86.73%, 84.85%, and 74.96%, respectively. None is exactly zero. In paired comparisons restricted to identical final answers, G0 has lower box NLL than base in 17.13% of 251 pairs, and than M5 in .66% of 304 pairs. These diagnostics concern only matched final answers. They neither establish global logit collapse nor isolate the training objective’s causal effect.

Length normalization also is not a universal guarantee of superior ranking. On the fresh Omni pooled-G0 cells, differences between tail10 and answer-mean AUROC are small and their paired intervals include zero. The tail-versus-length advantages are .2198 [.0989,.3356][.0989,.3356] for 4B4K, .1550 [.0474,.2649][.0474,.2649] for 4B8K, .1207 [.0483,.1946][.0483,.1946] for 8B4K, and .0685 [−.0018,.1396][-.0018,.1396] for 8B8K. Thus the strong failure of cumulative NLL on conservative 4B models establishes that length can confound a sum; it does not establish that tail10 is the best score in every cell.

C.2 Calibration variability and original gate failures

The retrospective 5,000-resplit review of original 8B DAPO 4K box-score policies found that both primary marginal wrong-answer targets were exceeded in 37.24% of splits. Both realized wrong-answer rates were at least as large as those of the original fixed split in 12.72%; the two rates had correlation .8329. This finite-pool description of correlated calibration fluctuation leaves the failed gates and the separate evidence of poor score ranking under OOD representation shift intact.

The S1 calibration-size analysis uses 2,000 family repartitions per configuration. DAPO uses CAL sizes 50, 100, 200, 300, and 500 from its 1,000 released families; Omni uses 50, 100, 200, and 300 from 600. At 8B4K and α=.065\alpha=.065, DAPO’s TEST-WW SD decreases from 2.573 to 1.187 pp, with mean 6.407% at CAL500; Omni’s decreases from 2.708 to 1.581 pp, with mean 6.307% at CAL300. Changing TEST denominators, discreteness, and all-pass cutoffs affect these curves. The table retains all 72 configurations: one curve has increased endpoint SD, and five are not nonincreasing across intermediate sizes.

Track B’s 28/36 and 8/36 counts include nine individual model arms, two budgets, and targets .065/.10, using tail10 only. Pooled-G0 rows, alternative scores, other targets, and Track A are excluded. Two conspicuous pooled exceedances at α=.10\alpha=.10 are 4B Omni8K W=11.83%W=11.83\% and 8B Omni8K W=12.00%W=12.00\%. Reporting these single-split outcomes together with the resplit means preserves the distinction between an expected risk guarantee and realized finite-test attainment.

For tail10 LTT on DAPO, the numbers issued at targets .10/.15/.20/.30 are 4/18, 12/18, 15/18, and 18/18; their TEST upper-bound attainments are 4, 12, 14, and 15. For answer mean, issuance is 5/18, 11/18, 13/18, and 18/18, with upper-bound attainments 4, 11, 12, and 14. Every issued DAPO setting has empirical TEST conditional error below its target. Each score issues three Omni policies, all at target .30; all empirical errors meet target, with zero tail10 and one answer-mean TEST upper-bound attainment. These counts describe repeated analyses of shared families, not independent replications.

C.3 Penalty and selection diagnostics

The pooled G0 comparisons in the main text retain both training seeds. For a same-seed reference, DAPO4K G041 has R=40.4%R=40.4\%, W=19.4%W=19.4\%, and truncation 36.6%, versus G141 at 29.4%, 10.2%, and 58.2%. Their mean sampled output counts are 3,429 and 3,628. S3A and S3B each have only one training seed, limiting conclusions about reproducibility across runs. The first/last-ten-update training truncation means are 64.92/62.73% for G1 and 63.75/47.27% for G041. The evidence is weaker reduction in budget exhaustion, not monotonic growth in training truncation (Figure 8).

After matched 4K CRC, pooled G0 minus S3A net-score differences are 5.6 pp [1.0,10.2][1.0,10.2] and 9.4 pp [4.3,14.6][4.3,14.6] on DAPO at .065 and .10; the corresponding differences versus S3B are 5.0 pp [.5,9.6][.5,9.6] and 9.0 pp [4.2,13.8][4.2,13.8]. On Omni, differences versus S3A are 2.5 pp [−2.0,7.17][-2.0,7.17] and 3.67 pp [−1.33,8.83][-1.33,8.83]; differences versus S3B are 3.83 pp [−.17,8.0][-.17,8.0] and 4.33 pp [−.67,9.67][-.67,9.67]. For DAPO at .065, realized WW is 7.1% for G0, 9.6% for S3A, and 10.2% for S3B. Equal nominal targets need not produce equal realized TEST risk, so the net differences should be read with the operating points.

The 455-point G0 risk–coverage file orders thresholds using CAL and evaluates them on TEST. Seven raw supplementary-arm points lie below its observed coverage/error frontier; DAPO8K S3B is the exception described in the main text. Selecting a preferred TEST point from this sweep is descriptive and receives no independent selective-policy guarantee. The full transition matrices retain right, wrong, truncation, explicit abstention, and other invalid outcomes separately.

C.4 White-box comparison and backend uncertainty

The entropy-versus-Native post hoc analysis joins exactly 500 DAPO TEST family identifiers, verifies the individual seed counts against the frozen A2 cuts, averages within family, and applies 20,000 multinomial family resamples with RNG seed 20261122. The supplied verifier reproduces the reported Δ​R\Delta R, Δ​W\Delta W, and Δ​Net\Delta\mathrm{Net} intervals. These intervals condition on calibration cuts, replayed trajectories, and the two trained policies; they do not include full training or calibration-refit variation. Reported generation times exclude the separate pass that extracts entropy features.

Backend behavioral comparisons contain 144 metric rows corresponding to 48 cells: 32 vLLM cells at n=50n=50 and 16 HF cells at n=4n=4, with separate R/W/UR/W/U intervals per cell. In the vLLM subset, two RR intervals, two WW intervals, and three UU intervals exclude zero; these occupy six distinct cells. For example, 4B G0 on Omni TEST at 4K has a wrong-answer change interval of [−16,−2][-16,-2] pp. Short fixed-token reconstruction probes and these finite-sample behavior checks are different forms of evidence; neither implies exact equality of backend generation distributions.

Appendix D Exploratory A100 pilots

All results in this appendix are small-sample exploratory checks. They do not enter the main empirical claims or confirmatory gates. The local training configuration uses four families and four rollouts per family per update, in contrast to the mainline 16-by-eight regimen. The completed Qwen runs train 4B G0/G1 and 8B G0/G0+KL/G0-multibudget for 12 updates, 192 trajectories, and 48 family exposures per arm. The KL coefficient is .02 with the frozen base distribution; the multibudget arm alternates 4K and 8K by update. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B has two G0 seeds and one G1 seed, each trained for 25 updates, 400 trajectories, and 100 family exposures. Earlier saved tiers are four and 12 updates; the planned 50-update tier was not completed. Final matched evaluation tiers have 16 CAL and 16 TEST families per domain; earlier tiers contain four. These exposures, model initializations, and serving paths differ from the Tinker mainline. They cannot establish cross-family replication, a reliable KL effect, or the benefit of multibudget training. The nineteen archived checkpoints total 6,155,082,568 bytes.

D.1 Operating points from the completed local-training tiers

Tables 10 and 11 report the final completed local checkpoints: 12 updates for the Qwen arms and 25 for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B. Every row has 16 matched TEST families and is calibrated on the corresponding 16 CAL families. The Qwen checkpoints have 192 training rollouts over 48 family exposures; the Llama checkpoints have 400 rollouts over 100 exposures. These locally trained models are distinct from the archived 50-update Tinker policies. All 32 final-tier ExtBF cells and all 12 final-tier Native Llama cells are included; earlier saved tiers remain separate in the raw artifact.

The reference for a G0 row is the same base model. The reference for G1, G0+KL, or G0+multi is local G041 at the same update tier, decoder, domain, and cap. Paired differences use the same 16 TEST families, even if the reference has a larger generation roster. The supplied pointwise family-bootstrap intervals condition on fitted CAL thresholds. A single changed outcome moves a rate by 6.25 pp, and a degenerate interval on an unchanged small panel does not imply zero population effect. The intervals exclude training-seed variation and are not corrected for multiple comparisons.

At CAL size 16, both targets .065 and .10 permit zero calibration wrong submissions under the corrected CRC rule; all displayed .10 cuts and operating points therefore equal their .065 counterparts. CAL size four in the earliest tier cannot support a nontrivial fit at either target and uses the all-reject fallback. The observed policies illustrate the limits of these small panels. For example, the 8B KL arm at Omni 8K gains four raw correct submissions over local G0, but its displayed calibrated subset has zero correct and one wrong submission. Neither this isolated contrast nor the local third-family outcomes establish a general KL effect, multibudget benefit, or cross-family replication.

The exact run identifiers and counts are in generation_summary.json, generation_crc.json, and mechanism_contrasts.json under the A100 supplement’s results directory. The training exposure and saved-tier index are in training_summary.json. The audit joins these records by complete run key and retains the raw per-cell contrasts in the accompanying numerical ledger.

D.2 Two-draw versus single-long-rollout pilot

The two-draw pilot compares two 4K generations with a single 8K generation on 16 TEST families per model and domain. Maj@2 resolves a tie using the first draw; strict agreement is a distinct policy that submits only on agreement. Counts below use the same 16 families in each row.

In these four small panels, the single 8K run uses fewer sampled tokens than the pair of 4K runs, by 13.8%, 8.4%, 21.0%, and 19.9%, respectively, relative to the two-draw token total. These observations do not compare prefix-shared branching, establish a general ranking of multi-sample reasoning, or estimate a population risk guarantee. The complete checkpoint/exposure index and pointwise local contrasts are preserved in the evidence bundle.

Appendix E Matched qualitative cases

The following twelve cases preserve the six matched-case categories in the released evidence. They are selected illustrations, not a random sample or an estimate of category prevalence. Every displayed passage is a contiguous verbatim substring of the archived terminal output; full questions, endings, family identifiers, and numerical metadata are in data/matched_cases.json. Scores and cutoffs are rounded only for display; acceptance uses the stored full-precision values and strict S<τS<\tau. A case-specific cutoff applies to the primary observed arm only. Paired responses document raw behavior and are not evaluated against a different model’s cutoff. Invalid or truncated responses are always rejected. The reference answer and tolerant R/W/UR/W/U label determine the recorded outcome; an excerpt does not independently validate every step of the generated argument. All examples use the 4K cap. For the Omni G0 cases, the shown cuts are the transferred DAPO cuts at α=.065\alpha=.065.
